script:
## [00:00] Nine o'clock, Vile Parle

It is a little before nine in the morning in Vile Parle, a suburb of Mumbai. In a small kitchen, a woman closes a steel lunchbox. Rice, dal, two rotis, a vegetable. She puts it in a cloth bag and hangs it by the door.
A man in a white cap collects it. He does not ask where it is going. He does not need to. He looks at the lid. There is a mark painted on it. A colour, a number, two letters.
By ten, the box is on a railway platform, in a wooden crate with thirty others. The train comes. It stops for less than a minute. The crate goes on.
By half past twelve, the box is on a desk in an office building in the south of the city. Nobody signed for it. Nobody phoned to ask where it was.
By six in the evening, the empty box is back in the same kitchen.

## [00:55] The question

In the years before 2020, this happened well over a lakh times a day, every working day. No software. Almost no paper. No owner watching. And most of the men who built it had very little schooling.
So here is the question for this episode. How do you run work at that scale when the work does not live in anyone's head?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [01:30] Five thousand men, one city

Let me give you the size of the job first.
The men are called dabbawalas. A dabba is a lunchbox. A dabbawala is the man who carries it.
In the twenty years before 2020 there were about five thousand of them in Mumbai. Forbes counted five thousand in 1998. Harvard counted the same number in 2012.
How many boxes they move depends on who you ask. Forbes said one lakh seventy-five thousand a day. Harvard counted more than one lakh thirty thousand, each one carried back the same afternoon. The association itself says two lakh. I will give you the range, not the biggest number, because the range is what the sources support.
Stefan Thomke, the Harvard professor who studied them, worked out what that means. More than two lakh sixty thousand handoffs in about six hours. Every working day. Six days a week.
Now think about the city. Mumbai has more than a crore of people. Its addresses are hard even for a taxi driver. Buildings have names, not numbers. Offices move from floor to floor.
And think about the men. Most come from the same belt of villages around Pune, often brought in by a brother, a cousin or a friend. For most of this history, they had very little schooling. Harvard found that only about fifteen in a hundred had been to junior high school. A long written address was not something this system could rely on.

## [03:00] The desk you know

Now let me bring this home.
Picture a firm of forty people in Indore. A trading business, or a small factory. Orders come in on the phone and on WhatsApp. The owner knows every customer. He knows which order is urgent, and which customer will shout. He knows which driver is on leave this week.
All of that is in his head. So every question comes to him. The accountant asks. The dispatch man asks. The salesman asks. And when the owner wants to know where something stands, he has to ask as well. He picks up the phone and types the same two words he typed yesterday: "Ho gaya?"
[your own line]
That owner is the memory of the business. He is also its follow-up department. And he usually finds out last, when the customer calls to complain.
Sometimes the person watching this is not the owner but the son or daughter who has joined the firm. You can see the problem clearly. You also know your father built this business by holding all of it in his head, and that it worked. The question is not whether he worked hard enough. He did. The question is where the work should live when the business is bigger than one head.
The dabbawalas had five thousand men and more than a lakh boxes a day, and nobody in that position. No single head held the whole city. The question is how.

## [04:30] Why the usual answers would fail

When a business grows, the owner usually reaches for one of three answers.
The first is a register, or these days a piece of software. Write everything down. But you cannot ask a man on a crowded platform to read a ledger. There is no time, and for many of these men, reading was never the easy part.
The second is the phone. Call and check. But for most of this history there were no phones in the work at all. Even in 2012, Harvard noted that the system ran without computers or mobile phones.
The third is a good manager. One sharp person who holds it all together. But a manager is still a single head. Five thousand men cannot all ask one person where a box is.
So the dabbawalas had to do something else. They had to put the information where every man could see it, at the moment he needed it. And they had to make the work run on a clock that nobody could argue with.

## [06:00] Five mechanisms

Here is how it works. I will show you five mechanisms. A code on the lid. A relay with fixed handoffs. A train that sets the clock. Two checks on every journey. And small groups that share the work, the money and the gaps.
None of these is clever on its own. What matters is how they fit together.

## [06:30] Mechanism one: the code on the lid

Start with the lid.
Every box carries a short code, painted by hand. Harvard describes it in three parts. Let me read you one lid.
In the middle, large and bold, is a number. That number is the area the box is going to. Say it is three. Three stands for the station nearest the office, at the far end of the line.
Along the rim, smaller, are three marks. First, a number for the man who will deliver it at the far end. Say nine. Then two or three letters for the building. Say E X, for an office tower. Then the floor. Say twelve.
And then there is a colour, and sometimes a shape. That tells you where the box started. Say a red circle for the home station, Vile Parle. Some lids also carry letters for the pickup area, such as V L P.
So this one lid says: from Vile Parle, to area three, to man nine, to building E X, floor twelve.
This is an illustration. Real codes vary from group to group. But the shape of the code is the same.
There is a second, quieter signal as well. Customers use cloth bags of different colours and shapes. Harvard noted that this helps the men pick out a box in a pile. Nobody designed that from the top. It grew because it made the next man's job easier.
Now notice what is not on the lid. No name. No street. No phone number. Not even a return address. The return trip works because the same man collects from the same homes every day. He knows where the box goes back.
Why so little? Thomke's answer is simple. A full address would clutter the lid and slow down sorting. A man on a platform has seconds. He needs to read the box at a glance, by colour and by number. So the code carries exactly what the next man needs for his step, and nothing more.
This is the answer to our first question. Where does the work live? It lives on the box. Not in the owner's head, and not in the delivery man's head. On the thing itself, where anyone holding it can read it.

## [09:00] Mechanism two: the relay

The second mechanism is the relay. One box passes through several hands, and each handoff happens at a fixed place and a fixed time.
Here is one station, Vile Parle, as a 2005 account describes it. About eighty men, in four groups of twenty.
Between seven and nine, the men collect boxes from homes, on bicycles and on foot. Each man has his own homes. Every day, the same ones.
By ten, the boxes are at the station. They are laid out on the platform and sorted into crates by destination. That is the first sort.
Between ten and half past eleven, the crates ride the train south. On the train, the men regroup. They are no longer grouped by where they live. They are grouped by where the boxes are going.
At the destination station, the boxes are sorted again, by building and by delivery man. That is the second sort.
By half past twelve, the boxes are on desks.
From about two in the afternoon, the same chain runs backwards. Empty boxes are collected, sorted, put on trains, and they are home by about six.
Count the hands. The man who collects. The men who sort at the first station. The men on the train. The men who sort at the second station. The man who delivers. One box, several pairs of hands, every day, and no paperwork passing between them. The lid is the paperwork.
Every man in this chain does one short leg. He knows exactly where he picks up and exactly where he hands over. He does not need to know the whole city. He needs to know his leg.
That matters for a business like yours. In most firms, a job passes from sales to accounts to the store to dispatch. But nobody has fixed where and when it changes hands. So it waits on someone's table, and nobody knows it is waiting. The dabbawalas fixed the table. It is a platform, and the time is ten o'clock.

## [11:30] Mechanism three: the train sets the clock

The third mechanism is the train.
Mumbai's suburban railway runs to a timetable. The dabbawalas built their whole day around it. The train does not wait for anyone. Harvard noted that crates are loaded in about forty seconds at a major station, and about twenty at a smaller one.
Think about what that does. If a box is not on the platform when the train comes, it has missed its slot. There is no discussion. Everyone on that platform can see it.
This is the answer to our second question. How can anyone see the state of the work? Here, the state of a box is simply where it is. On the platform at ten, it is moving. Not on the platform at ten, it is late. Nobody has to ask.
It answers our third question too. Who finds out when something slips, and how fast? The next man in the chain. He is standing there, waiting for the crate. He finds out in minutes, not at the end of the month. Thomke makes exactly this point. The tight schedule makes it obvious at once when someone falls behind.
The loop reaches the customer as well. A household that keeps handing over the box late is warned. If it keeps happening, it is dropped. The rhythm protects everyone else's lunch.
Most businesses I see have no clock like this. A quote is due soon. A dispatch will go today. Without a fixed time, late is invisible until the customer calls. The train gave the dabbawalas a clock that nobody could argue with.

## [13:30] Mechanism four: two checks and a few hard rules

The fourth mechanism is how mistakes are caught.
Every box is sorted twice. Once at the station where it starts, and once at the station where it ends. A wrong crate at the first sort can be caught at the second, before the box reaches the wrong desk.
Then there are a few hard rules. Boxes must be about the same size. An oversized or unusual box costs extra, or is refused. Crates are standard. The supervisors, called mukadams, usually have more than ten years in the work. They handle the coding and the sorting, and they still carry boxes themselves. A man who keeps making mistakes is fined, and in the end let go.
Now, you may have heard that Forbes certified the dabbawalas as Six Sigma, with one mistake in six million deliveries. I want to be careful here. This story is repeated everywhere, and it is not quite true.
In August 1998, Forbes ran a short article. The association's president at the time, Ragunath Medge, told the reporter that mistakes happened about once every two months. He also said this: "If we made 10 mistakes a month, no one would use our service." The reporter did the arithmetic. One error in about eight million deliveries. Sixteen million, if you count the return trip.
That is a reporter's sum, built on one man's estimate. It is not a study. The article does not mention Six Sigma at all. Six Sigma is a quality method, not a certificate, and Forbes does not award it. Years later, the reporter said in an interview that Forbes never certified the dabbawalas. And the figure of one in six million has no source that I could find.
So what can we honestly say? The people closest to the work say mistakes are rare. Harvard called them extremely rare, and gave no number. That is enough. It is still remarkable, and it is true.

## [16:00] Mechanism five: small groups, shared money, spare men

The fifth mechanism is how the people are organised. Harvard found this the most important part of all.
There is no owner. Harvard counted about two hundred groups of around twenty-five men. Each group finds its own customers and collects its own fees. In the Vile Parle account, a group of twenty served about six hundred and seventy-five customers. It collected about one lakh rupees a month and split it equally. Every man had the same stake in every box.
The mukadams settle disputes inside the group. Elected committees meet every month and set price guidance by distance. A trust that every member pays into covers insurance, and things like replacing a stolen bicycle. So the small troubles that would land on an owner's desk in your firm have a place to go here.
Each group carries two or three spare men. They fill in wherever someone is missing. And every man is trained in every part of the work: collecting, sorting, the train, the money and the customers.
So, our fifth question. What happens when the owner is away? Here, there is no owner to be away. And when any one man is away, a spare man steps in. He reads the same lids and stands on the same platform at the same time. The work goes out.
New men join only when the group decides there is enough demand. A new man works six months on probation, learning on the route. Then he can buy into the group, for about ten times his expected monthly income. Harvard's example is seventy thousand rupees, for a man expecting seven thousand a month.
Think about what that new man needs on his first day. He does not need to know Mumbai. He does not need to remember a thousand addresses. He needs to read a colour and a number, and to be on the platform at ten. The system carries the rest.
The association dates all this to 1890, to a man called Mahadeo Havaji Bachche and about a hundred men from the villages near Pune. He died generations ago. The boxes went out the next morning, and for a century after.

## [17:20] Five questions, five answers

Let me put the five answers side by side.
Where does the work live? On the lid. How can anyone see its state? By where the box is at ten o'clock. Who finds out when it slips? The next man in the chain, within minutes. How are mistakes caught? By a second sort, before the box reaches the desk. And what happens when someone is away? A spare man reads the same lid.
Harvard's conclusion was that ordinary people, in a well-designed system, do extraordinary work. Thomke said the manager's job is to be the designer of that system.
There is one question left. What happened when it broke?

## [18:00] The day it breaks

Every system looks good on an ordinary Tuesday. The test is the day it breaks.
The dabbawalas have had two such tests on the public record. One they came through in two days. The other is still going on.

## [18:20] July 2005

On the twenty-sixth of July 2005, Mumbai flooded. Harvard records more than twenty-five inches of rain in twelve hours, with record high tides. The trains stopped. People were stranded at stations, on trains and on the roads.
The dabbawalas were stranded too. Their president was himself stuck on a train with ten other men, carrying empty boxes.
On the second day, before the city had properly restarted, the dabbawalas were back at work. They waded through the water to get the boxes home.
Notice what did not happen. Nobody waited for instructions from an office. Nobody needed to find the owner. Nobody had written a flood plan. They did not need one. Every man knew his leg, his handoff and his time. When the trains moved again, the system moved with them.
There is one more sign of how steady this system has been. In 2011, the dabbawalas stopped work for a day to join a public rally. Newspapers reported it as their first strike in a hundred and twenty years.

## [19:45] March 2020

The second test was harder, because it took away both things the system stands on. Offices full of people, and suburban trains.
In March 2020, the lockdown began and the service stopped. With no trains and no offices, there was nothing to carry. Housing societies would not let the men in to collect their fees. By July that year, more than four thousand dabbawalas had gone back to their villages. Some lost family members to the virus.
They were allowed back on local trains in October 2020. But the offices were still empty. In June 2021, the association said it had recovered about five per cent of its business. Its spokesman said the two thousand rupees the government had promised each man had not reached a single one of them. Men worked as security guards, in shops and as drivers to feed their families. Some carried restaurant meals instead of home-cooked lunch.
Here is where they stand now. A report by the Press Trust of India in June this year, quoting the association's president, put the number at about three thousand men, down from about five thousand. At the lowest point it was about fifteen hundred. Together they deliver a little over fifty thousand boxes a day. A BBC report in May cited the association's registered count at about fifteen hundred. The two figures may be counting different things. Either way, the number is roughly half what it was, or less.

## [21:30] What the test shows

So what does this test tell us?
It tells us the system itself did not fail. The code still works. The relay still works. A man back from his village could read a lid on his first morning back.
What failed was outside the system. The demand. Office workers stayed at home. Food apps arrived with discounts. And the one thing the dabbawalas never controlled, the railway, was shut for months.
This is the honest limit, and I want to say it plainly. The dabbawalas are not a company. They are an association of partners. Nobody owns it, and nobody invests in it. Earnings have always been modest. About three thousand two hundred rupees a month in 1998, according to Forbes. Fifteen to twenty-five thousand today, according to the 2026 report.
Harvard noted that the dabbawalas turned down ideas that would disturb the routine, from carrying advertising samples to buying motorcycles. The same discipline that made them reliable made it hard for them to change when the city changed.
A good system carries the work. It does not choose the market for you. That is still the owner's job.
I find that reassuring, not discouraging. It means the system is not the whole business. It is the part that frees the owner to think about the rest.

## [23:00] From Mumbai to your firm

Now let me bring this back to a business of fifteen to a hundred people. Not five thousand. Not Mumbai. Your firm, with your orders and your team.
I see four lessons. Each one comes from a moment in this story.

## [23:30] Lesson one: put the state on the work

The first lesson is the lid.
In the dabbawala system, the next step is written on the thing itself. Anyone holding the box knows where it goes next.
In most of the firms I meet, the next step lives in someone's head. An order comes in. The salesman knows the customer wants it by Thursday. The store knows one item is short. The owner knows the customer will call on Wednesday. None of this is written where the next person can see it.
So the lesson is this. Give every piece of work a home. A quote, an order, a dispatch, a client file. Each one needs three things written where anyone can see them. A name, meaning the person who owns the next step. A date. And the next step itself.
That is your lid. It does not need to be clever. It needs to be the same every time, and short enough to read at a glance.

## [24:45] Lesson two: fix the handoffs and the clock

The second lesson is the platform at ten o'clock.
The dabbawalas do not hand over boxes whenever they like. They hand over at a fixed place, at a fixed time. If the crate is not there, everyone sees it.
In a small firm, the handoff between sales and accounts, or between the store and dispatch, usually has no fixed time. It happens when someone remembers. So the job waits on a table, and nobody knows it is waiting.
Fix the clock. It does not have to be a train. It can be a time of day that everyone knows. Decide that dispatch slips reach the gate by four. Decide that the week's work is handed out on Monday morning, and that the score comes back on Friday. Then late is not a feeling. It is a fact that anyone can see, without the owner asking.

## [25:50] Lesson three: check at the handoff

The third lesson is the second sort.
The dabbawalas check every box twice, once when it leaves and once when it arrives. A mistake on the first platform is caught on the second. It never reaches the customer.
Most firms check at the end, when the customer complains. Or they ask the owner to check everything, which means the owner becomes the quality department as well as the follow-up department.
Put the check at the handoff instead, where the work changes hands and a second pair of eyes is already there. A quote is checked by a second person before it goes out. A dispatch is checked against the order at the gate, not after the truck has left. The check is small. It is the same every time. And it is not the owner.

## [26:50] Lesson four: spare hands, and a useful first day

The fourth lesson is the spare man.
Every dabbawala group carries two or three people who can step into any role. And every man is trained in every part of the work. So one absence stops nothing.
In a forty-person firm, one person on leave can stop a whole process. Because only he knows the client, or the supplier's terms, or which order is urgent.
So ask one question about each process. If this person is away tomorrow, can someone else pick up the work just by reading what is written? If the answer is no, the work lives in a person. Move it onto the job.
And when the work lives on the job, a new joiner can be useful on the first day. Like the dabbawala who only needs to read a colour and a number.
Think of the last person you hired. How long before they could act without asking you? If the answer is months, that is not a judgement on them. It tells you how much of the work is still unwritten.
You do not need to do all four at once. Start with one process. The one that brings the most questions to your desk.

## [28:00] What I do now

In my family's firm, VSP Consultants in Indore, we had the problem I described at the start. The work lived in a few heads, and the follow-ups lived with the owner. I trained as a designer, so I looked at it as a design problem, not a discipline problem. I designed a system where every piece of work has a home, with a name, a date and a next step, on one screen the whole team can see. The firm runs on it every day.
[your own line]
This is the work I do now, at Venture Drafters. We set up this kind of system for owner-led businesses, on your own sheet. We train your team on it, and we manage it with you. And we start with one process.
I do not think your firm should look like the dabbawalas. Your work is not a lunchbox, and your team is not five thousand men. But the questions are the same. Where does the work live? Who can see it? Who finds out when it slips? Those are design questions, and they have answers.
The dabbawalas never had software. They had a code, a clock, and a chain of people who could rely on the next handoff. That is the part worth borrowing.

script:
## [00:00] Cold open: the counter

A paint shop in a small town. Four o'clock in the afternoon. A woman has brought a shade card from home. Her finger is on one small square of colour. A soft green, the colour she wants for her daughter's room.
The shopkeeper does not go to the back. He does not phone the depot. He types a number into a machine on his counter. The machine pumps a few drops of this, a few drops of that, into a can of white paint. The can goes onto a shaker. A few minutes later she walks out with her green.
That shop does not stock her green. It never did. It stocks a few cans of base and a rack of colours. Everything else is made at the counter.

## [00:50] The question

Asian Paints shows two thousand two hundred shades on its current fan deck. No shop in India can keep two thousand two hundred shades, in four pack sizes, in every range.
So how does a paint company decide which colour to keep in which town, on which day? That is the question for this episode. The answer is not a bigger warehouse. It is a design decision, taken decades ago, and a habit of planning that most companies in India did not have.
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [01:30] Act 1: your own counter

Before we go to Asian Paints, let us start at your counter.
A customer calls. He wants a size you do not have. Or a finish. Or a grade. Or a colour. You have two choices, and both are bad. You say "not in stock", and he buys from the shop down the road. Or you start keeping everything, just in case. Then your godown fills with stock that does not move, and your money sits on the shelf.
Most owners I meet handle this from memory. Their own, or a trusted manager's. The manager knows that this item sells before Diwali. That one sells in the rains. This customer always wants the heavy gauge. When a dealer phones and asks, "Stock hai?", the answer comes from someone's head.
That works while the business is small enough to fit in one head. It stops working when the range grows, or the manager goes on leave, or you open a second godown. Then you find out last. The customer finds out first.

## [02:45] The size of the paint problem

Now take that problem and multiply it.
Paint comes in many ranges, from cheap distemper to premium emulsion. Each range comes in several pack sizes. Each one, in principle, comes in every shade on the card. And it is sold in tens of thousands of small shops, from metros to towns that are not on most maps.
Demand is not even. It rises before festivals. It falls in the rains. It is different in Tamil Nadu and in Punjab. A company that tried to stock every shade, in every size, in every town, would drown in paint. A company that stocked too little would lose the sale to the shop next door.
Every new shade on the card makes the problem worse. More choice for the customer means more ways for the shop to be wrong.
Asian Paints has been the largest paint company in India since 1967. It got there by solving this problem earlier, and more carefully, than anyone else in the trade. To see how, we have to go back to a garage.

## [04:00] A garage in wartime Bombay

1942. Bombay. The war has cut paint imports. Four friends rent a garage and start making paint. Their names are Champaklal Choksey, Chimanlal Choksi, Suryakant Dani and Arvind Vakil. The company's historian, Anupam Gupta, records a fifth early partner who put in money and later sold out. So the story of four friends is true, but it is not the whole cast.
They are young. They know how to sell paint better than how to make it. And the big market is closed to them. The foreign paint companies sell through a few large distributors in the cities, and those distributors decide which brands reach the shops.

## [04:40] The door they went around

So Asian Paints goes around the door. It sells directly to the shopkeeper, from its own depots. Accounts of the company's history say the first dealer was in Sangli, not in Bombay. Any shop that can pay on time can buy. By 1967 it is the largest paint maker in the country.
Here is the part most retellings skip. A wholesaler does two quiet jobs. He holds stock between the factory and the shop. And he guesses, from memory, what each shop will want next month.
For the shopkeeper, the new arrangement was attractive. He bought from the maker, not from a middleman. But for the company, it carried a hidden cost.
When Asian Paints cut out the wholesaler, it cut out the person doing the guessing. Now there was nobody between the depot and thousands of small shops. If a depot ran out of a fast-selling product before a festival, the company heard about it from an angry dealer.
So it had to know, itself, what each depot would need. Not roughly. Item by item. That is a planning problem. And in India, in the 1960s, almost nobody was solving planning problems with data.

## [06:00] Act 2: the system

Let us look at the system Asian Paints built. I will take it in five parts. A machine in an office. A plan for every item at every depot. Trucks that come every day. A machine on the counter. And a calendar.
For each part, I will tell you what is on the record, and what is only a good story. Because this company has attracted a lot of good stories.

## [06:30] Part one: the computer, and the folklore around it

If you read investor blogs, you will find a precise story. In 1970, Asian Paints bought India's first supercomputer. A named model. Eight crore rupees. Before ISRO and before the IITs.
I tried to trace that story to a source. I could not. None of those blogs points to a company document or a record from the time.
Here is what does hold up. Forbes India reported that Asian Paints bought its first mainframe computer in the 1970s, when computers were almost unknown in Indian business, and soon used it to forecast demand. Anupam Gupta, who wrote the company's history, also places the computer in the 1970s, and says it was among the first in India to buy one. He also says Esso and the Tatas bought mainframes in the same period. So "among the first" is fair. "The first" cannot be shown from any record, and I will not say it.
Gupta adds one detail that tells you how serious the decision was. He says the machine cost about a tenth of the company's total assets.
Think about that in your own terms. Imagine spending a tenth of everything your firm owns on a machine whose main job is to tell you what your customers will buy next month. That is not a technology decision. That is a decision about how you want to run the business. Data instead of a wholesaler's memory.
In his account, the point of the machine was to plan ahead. To know what dealers in a region would need, by season and by colour, before the dealers themselves had noticed their shelves were thin.
He also says the computer was used to run a discount for dealers who paid within thirty days. So the same machine that planned the stock also tracked the money. The two were never separate.

## [08:30] Part two: a plan for every item at every depot

The first question we ask in every story is simple. Where does the work live?
At Asian Paints, the work of deciding what goes where lives in a plan. Not in a sales officer's head.
The company says it has run an integrated planning system since 1999. One system that links the forecast, the factory and the delivery. In 2009 it chose planning software from a company called i2 to forecast about fifteen hundred items and to plan buying, making, moving and stocking across factories, warehouses and depots together. A planner from the company wrote in 2016 about using near real-time information to predict changes in demand within a month.
Today, the company's annual report says its forecasts are made at the depot and item level. It uses historical sales, real-time data, market information and statistical models, including machine learning. The factory plan, the shipping plan and the buying plan all follow from that forecast.
Notice the unit. Not India. Not a region. One item, at one depot.
Compare that with most firms I see. The forecast, if there is one, is a feeling. The owner says, "Last year was good, order a little more." Nobody writes down for which item, or for which customer, or for which godown. At Asian Paints, the feeling was replaced by a number in a cell, and the cell had an address.
That is the real answer to "which colour in which area". The company does not guess for the country and then divide. It builds the forecast from the bottom, item by item, place by place. A spike in one district shows up in that district's numbers. It does not disappear inside a national total.

## [10:30] Part three: trucks that come every day

A forecast is only useful if the trucks behind it are fast. So, the second question. How can anyone see the state of the work? And the third. Who finds out when something slips?
Look at the network, year by year. In 2013, Forbes India counted about thirty-five thousand dealers. In 2019, the company told investors it had more than sixty thousand retailers and one hundred and thirty-five depots. In 2021, its head of supply chain described about seventy-five thousand dealers, served directly from eight factories and one hundred and forty-three warehouses.
And here is the number I find most useful. In larger towns, a dealer who orders in the morning gets the paint the same day. In the largest cities, a dealer can get two deliveries a day.
Think about what that does to the shopkeeper. He does not need to guess a month ahead. He orders what sold this morning, and it comes this evening. The guessing moves up the chain, to the depot, where it can be done with data.
In that same 2019 presentation, the company said its depots were serving more customers while its finished-goods stock had come down. More shops, less stock. That is what a short cycle buys you.
Money moves on the same short cycle. In 2019 the company said seventy percent of its sales were on three-day payment.
And the state of the work is visible. The company tracks its order fill rate. That means how much of each dealer order was supplied in full. A depot that keeps missing items shows up in that number. Nobody has to phone the head office to complain. The number complains for them.
So when a forecast is wrong, the company finds out within days. Not at the end of the quarter. Not from the owner walking the market.

## [12:35] Part four: the machine on the counter

Now the part that answers the question I started with. How do they choose which shade to keep in which town?
For most shades, they do not choose. They do not keep them at all.
Asian Paints introduced computerised colour matching in the mid-1970s. By 2019 it had more than forty-six thousand ColourWorld outlets. That is its own tinting system, placed in dealers' shops. It was adding about four thousand a year.
Here is how a tinting machine works. The shop keeps a few base paints. Think of them, for illustration, as a white, a mid-tone and a deep base. And it keeps a rack of concentrated colours. Systems like this usually run on two to four bases and about a dozen colourants. Every shade on the card has a recipe stored in the machine. Which base. How many drops of each colour. The machine measures them exactly, pumps them into the base can, and the shaker mixes it. A set like this can make more than a thousand shades.
The supply-chain word for this is postponement. In plain words: keep the common part in stock, and make the special part at the last moment, after the customer has chosen.
Look at what that does to the planning problem. The question used to be: which of two thousand two hundred shades should this shop keep? Now the question is: how many cans of each base, and how many bottles of each colour? That is a short list. It can be forecast. And a wrong guess about a shade costs nothing, because the shade was never made.
This is the fourth question. How are errors caught before they reach the customer? The best answer is a design that removes the error. The most expensive mistake in this trade is the wrong shade, made in bulk, sitting in the wrong town. With tinting at the counter, that mistake cannot happen.
The company keeps refining the rest. In 2023-24 it said a new inventory tool cut its stock norms by about five percent, while service improved. It is also building regional centres for slow-moving items, so the uncertain tail of the range is held once, centrally, not at every depot.
One thing I want to be careful about. You may read that the tinting machines send their data back to head office to drive the forecast. It is plausible. I could not find a public source that says so. So I am not saying it.

## [15:25] Part five: the calendar

The last part is the calendar.
Paint demand follows festivals, and India's festivals do not fall on the same day everywhere. The company's head of supply chain explained it in 2021. Diwali, in October and November, drives demand in the North and the West. Harvest festivals, in February and March, drive it in other regions.
Rain works the other way. Nobody paints an outside wall in a downpour. In the July to September quarter of 2024, the company reported a small fall in volumes and named persistent rains and floods as one reason.
So a depot in the North needs more stock in October. A depot in the South may need it in February. A depot in a flood-hit district needs less in August. One national plan could never get all three right.
There is a lovely story from the company's history, told in Gupta's book and retold by The Ken. Sales of small cans spiked around Trichy every winter. Someone went to find out why. Farmers were painting the horns of their cattle for Pongal. I tell it as company lore, not as a documented case. But it shows exactly why the forecast is built depot by depot. A national total would never have shown you cattle horns in Trichy.

## [16:50] When the owner is away

The fifth question in this series is the hardest for any founder. What happens when the owner is away?
At Asian Paints, the founders were not there forever. Arvind Vakil died early. Champaklal Choksey led the company for fifty-five years and died in 1997. By 1999 the company was running its integrated planning system.
I want to be honest. No source I found says the founder's death led to the planning system. The dates sit close together, and that is all. What the record does show is this. The company kept its lead after the founding generation. Paint kept reaching the right depot. That only happens when the knowledge of what sells where has been moved out of one person's head and into a plan that anyone can read.

## [17:45] The five answers

So, five answers. The work lives in a forecast, one item at one depot. The state of the work shows in the order fill rate. The feedback loop is a daily order and a same-day truck. Errors are prevented by making the shade at the counter. And the plan kept running after the founder.
Now the sixth question. What happened when it broke?

## [18:00] Act 3: the test

Every system looks good in a normal year. The question is what it does in a bad one. A founder on leave. A big order that goes wrong. A new rival. A year when nothing sells.
For Asian Paints, the clearest test on the public record is the spring of 2020. I chose it because the company's own people have described, on the record, what they did.

## [18:30] April 2020

March 2020. India locks down. Shops close. Many painters leave the cities.
The company's chief executive later described April as completely washed out. For April to June 2020, the company's revenue fell by about forty-three percent compared with the year before.
Then the problems get specific. Some dealers are allowed to open. But the company warehouses that normally serve them sit inside containment zones. The trucks cannot leave.

## [19:00] The workaround

So the company does something it would never plan in a normal year. It supplies those dealers directly from its factories. A dealer who normally takes small orders now receives up to half a truckload at a time. Paint that reaches an open shop is better than paint stuck behind a closed warehouse door.
That decision tells you something. You can only route around a closed warehouse if you know, item by item, what each shop needs and what each warehouse was holding. A company running on memory would not know where to send the paint.
It also has to keep its own factories running while keeping its workers safe. That is not a small thing in 2020.
At the same time, it uses what it has. Its head of supply chain described how the company began making hand sanitiser from raw materials it already held, and then a painting service with sanitising, so painters could enter homes safely.

## [20:05] The recovery, and a straight answer

Demand came back sooner than many expected. It came back first in smaller towns. People were at home, looking at their own walls.
From July to September 2020, the company's decorative volumes grew eleven percent. From October to December, they grew thirty-three percent.
Here is the moment I find most telling. On the results call, an analyst asked whether those numbers were inflated by pushing stock onto dealers before a price rise. That is an old trick. Fill the channel, and the quarter looks good.
The chief executive said there was "no inventory in the network" that had gone up. He said the company had not pushed stock onto retailers, and believed what it sold had been sold on to customers.
You can only answer that question with confidence if you can see the stock in the channel. That is what a planning system gives you. Not luck. A straight answer.

## [21:15] A second test, still running

I do not want to tell this as a story where the system always wins. There is a second test, and it is still running.
In February 2024, the Aditya Birla Group launched a paint business called Birla Opus, with a commitment of ten thousand crore rupees. It described the new plants as adding forty percent to the industry's capacity.
In the October to December quarter of 2024, Asian Paints reported decorative volumes up just 1.6 percent, revenue down 7.8 percent and a lower margin. The company itself named weak demand, customers moving to cheaper products and a weak festive season.
A planning system does not stop a competitor. It does not make customers spend. What it does is show you the damage early, in detail, depot by depot. What you do about it is still a management decision.

## [22:10] What the test shows

So here is the sixth answer. When it broke, in 2020, the plan told the company what each shop needed, even when the usual route was closed. When demand returned, the company could say plainly that it had not stuffed its dealers. And when a rival arrived with deep pockets, the numbers showed the pressure quickly, even if they could not make it go away.
Think about your own firm in April 2020. Did you know, that week, what was in each godown, what each customer had on order, and what you could still deliver? Or did you find out by phoning around, one person at a time?
That is what a system is for. Not to prevent bad years. To make sure you see them clearly, and early, and not last.

## [23:00] Act 4: what this means for a business of 15 to 100 people

You do not run a paint company with seventy-five thousand dealers. You may run a trading firm with forty people and two godowns. Or a factory with three hundred items and fifty regular customers. You do not need a mainframe, or machine learning, or a planning team. But four ideas from this story travel well to your size.

## [23:20] Lesson one: split your range into bases and shades

Remember the tinting machine. A few bases, many shades.
Look at your own list the same way. Your bases are the items many orders need. The standard sizes. The common grade. The plain carton before printing. The grey fabric before dyeing. The bare frame before the finish. These you must keep in stock, always.
Your shades are the variations. The special finish. The custom print. The rare size one customer asks for twice a year. These you can make or order when the customer confirms. On the quote, you write the lead time, and you stop pretending you keep them.
Start small. Take your top fifty items by sales and mark each one, base or shade. You do not need to sort all three thousand codes in your software on the first day.
When you do this honestly, many owners find their list of "must keep" items is much shorter than their godown suggests. And the question "what should we stock?" becomes a question you can actually answer.

## [24:40] Lesson two: plan each item at each place

Remember the depot-by-item forecast. Asian Paints does not plan India. It plans one item at one depot.
In your firm, that means a row for each item at each place. If you have one godown in Indore and one in Pithampur, the same item gets two rows. If you supply three large customers on a schedule, each one may need its own row for the items they buy.
A total hides the problem. "We have two hundred boxes" means nothing if all two hundred are in the wrong godown. And the customer in Pithampur does not care how many boxes you have in Indore. One row per item per place is the smallest change that makes the problem visible.

## [25:30] Lesson three: order what sold, every week

Remember the morning order and the evening truck. The dealer does not guess a month ahead. He replaces what sold.
At your size, a weekly rhythm is enough. Here is what it looks like on a sheet. One row per item per place. Then these columns. Base or shade. The most you want to hold. What is in stock on Monday morning. What sold last week. What to order this week, which is usually what sold, topped up to your limit. Who places the order. And a column that says done, with a date.
Here is an invented example, to make it concrete. A fastener trader. One row: a standard bolt, at the Indore godown, marked base. The most he wants to hold is four hundred boxes. On Monday there are one hundred and ninety. Last week, two hundred sold. So this week, he orders two hundred. The rare stainless bolt, marked shade, has no stock limit at all. It is ordered only against a confirmed customer order.
On Monday, the sheet is the hand-out. The person whose name is on the row places the order. Nobody waits for the owner to remember.
On Friday, the sheet gives the score. How many times this week did we say "not in stock"? Which items are sitting far above the limit? Those two numbers tell you more about your stock than any long report.
And one rule from the 2020 story. Never push stock onto a customer to make a month look good. If the sheet is honest, you will not need to.

## [27:15] Lesson four: write the season down

Remember the cattle horns in Trichy. Somebody noticed a pattern, and the plan took it in.
Every business has its season. A rush before Diwali. A dead month in the rains. A wedding season. A school reopening. A financial year end. In most firms, this lives in one experienced person's memory.
Write it down. Add a column for the month, and keep last year's sales beside this year's. After one year, the sheet remembers what you used to carry in your head. After two, you can see whether this Diwali is better or worse than the last one, item by item. Before a busy month, raise the limit on the items that move. After it, bring it back down. Your senior manager still knows the market better than any sheet. The sheet just means that knowledge stays when he is on leave.

## [28:00] Close

So, which shade, in which town, on which day? Most shades are not kept anywhere. They are made at the counter, in a few minutes, from a few bases. The bases and the fast items are forecast for each depot, one item at a time. Trucks refill the shops every day, and twice a day in the biggest cities. And the calendar, by region, is written into the plan.
Asian Paints chose data over a wholesaler's memory long before it was easy. Then it went further, and removed most of the guessing at the root, by making the shade at the counter.
None of this is clever. It is patient. A company that chose, more than fifty years ago, to put what it knew about its customers into a place anyone could read, and kept doing it.
This is the work I do now. I designed my family's firm's system first, at VSP Consultants in Indore, and we run on it every day. In my family's firm, [your own line]. Now I help owners of firms with fifteen to one hundred people do the same, one process at a time, on their own sheet. For a trader or a manufacturer, a sensible first process is this one: what to keep, what to order, and who orders it on Monday.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.

## [29:50] End card

Thank you for watching. Next week, another business, and another system that carried it further than one person could.

script:
## [00:00] Cold open: the fifth of June

It is the fifth of June, 2015. In New Delhi, the global chief executive of Nestlé stands in front of the press. He says the noodles are safe. The same day, India's food regulator orders every variant of Maggi to be withdrawn and recalled.
Across the country, about three and a half million shops sell this packet. Some are supermarkets. Most are small shops, with a few packets hanging in a net by the counter.
Within days, all of it has to come back. Every carton in every warehouse. Every loose packet on every shelf. The chain that carried this packet out for thirty years now has to carry it back.
On the back of each packet there is one small line of print. A batch code. A date of manufacture. A best-before date. On the worst day in this brand's history, that line of print matters more than the advertising, the reach and the thirty years of goodwill.

## [01:05] The question

I want to ask one question in this episode. What is a system for, when the worst day comes?
Not on a normal Monday. On the day someone outside your business asks a hard question, and wants the answer today. And whether your records can give that answer, or only your memory.
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [01:35] Act 1: Thirty years of reach

Let me start with the good years, because this is not a story about a weak company.
Nestlé launched Maggi noodles in India in 1983. At the time there was no quick hot snack a mother could make between school and dinner. A samosa or a kachori could not be made in a few minutes. Maggi offered a hot snack in two minutes.
One of the people on the launch team has described how they thought about it. Children were the audience. The mother was the person who decided. Few homes watched much television then, so they sold through displays in shops and through promotions at schools and in parks.
It worked slowly, and then completely. Two minutes became part of how the country spoke. Hostel rooms. Hill-station stalls. Late nights in offices. For many children, the first thing they learned to cook. A packet that cost a few rupees became a habit in millions of homes.
You will hear many large numbers about this brand in feature stories. A lot of them cannot be traced to any source. In this episode I will give you only the ones that can.

## [02:55] The machine behind the packet

Behind the promise was a distribution system that very few companies in India could match.
By 2015, Maggi was made in five factories. It moved through thirty-eight distribution centres that Nestlé ran directly. From there it went to about fourteen hundred distributors. And from them, by Nestlé's own estimate, to about three and a half million shops.
That is the reach that put a yellow packet in a hill-station stall, a college hostel and a kirana shop in a small town in Madhya Pradesh.
How much of the market did it hold? The answer depends on who measured. Euromonitor put it at sixty-three percent of the noodle market in 2014. Nestlé India later said its share before the crisis was about seventy-five percent. Nielsen data, as reported in the press, said seventy-seven percent in January 2015. One brokerage said about eighty. Whichever number you take, this was the brand that defined the category.

## [03:50] Your desk in this story

Now, you may be thinking, I run a forty-person firm in Indore. I am not Nestlé.
That is true. Nestlé India is a listed company. It had more than seven thousand employees. It has a global parent with its own laboratories and lawyers. You will never face a national regulator and a High Court in the same summer.
But think about the shape of the problem.
You make something, or you deliver something. It goes out through people you do not fully see. A dealer. A sub-dealer. A site supervisor. A junior in your office who sends the file to the client.
One day a customer calls and says, something is wrong with what you sent. Which lot was it? Who else got material from the same lot? What did your quality check show that day? Who signed it off?
In many firms, the answer to each of those questions is a person. The owner remembers. The dispatch man remembers. The accountant can find it, if you give him two days.
And the owner, meanwhile, is on the phone. To the dispatch man. To the dealer. To the supervisor. The same question, in different words, all afternoon. Every owner knows the call that ends with one tired question: "Ho gaya?"
I have sat at that desk. In my family's firm, before we designed our system, the answer to most questions was a person. Usually the same person.

## [05:30] The work that has no home

That is what I mean when I say work needs a home. A name. A date. A next step. A place anyone can look, without asking.
Maggi had that home for every packet that left the factory. What the year 2015 tested was everything that came after the factory. And whether the records could answer a question that came from outside, in the form the outsider wanted.
Let us look at the system piece by piece.

## [06:00] Act 2: Five pieces of one system

Every story in this series is read through the same six questions.
Where does the work live? How can anyone see the state of it? Who finds out when something slips, and how fast? How are mistakes caught before they reach the customer? What happens when the person at the top is not there? And what happened when it broke?
For Maggi, the sixth question is the reason we are here. So let us take the first five, one at a time, and look at the piece of the system that answers each.

## [06:40] Mechanism one: the line of print on the pack

The first mechanism is the smallest. It is the batch code.
Every packet of Maggi carries a batch number, a date of manufacture and a best-before date. In a food business, that line of print is the home of the work. It tells you which plant made it, on which day, in which run.
Here is how well it worked in this story. In April 2015, the food authorities in Lucknow asked Nestlé to recall one batch. Nestlé could say exactly what that batch was. It was made in February 2014. It was about two lakh packs. And its best-before date had already passed, in November 2014.
That is a good record. One batch, named, dated and sized, on demand.
Think about what a batch record in any food plant has to connect. The flour, the oil, the spice mix, each with its own supplier lot. The line it ran on. The shift. The checks done before release. When a question comes about one packet, a good batch record lets you walk backwards to every input, and forwards to every carton.
That is all traceability means. It is not a software word. It is the ability to walk the chain in both directions.
So the first question of this series, where does the work live, has a clear answer at the factory gate. It lives on the pack and in the batch record. Not in someone's memory.

## [08:15] Mechanism two: the chain that pushes

The second mechanism is the distribution chain.
From factory to distribution centre, Nestlé could see everything. From distribution centre to distributor, it had an invoice for every carton.
But look at the last step. Nestlé estimated that about half of the three and a half million shops that sold Maggi were not served directly by its own distributor network. They bought through wholesalers and smaller traders. The company could not see them.
This is the second question of the series. How can anyone see the state of the work? Up to the distributor, the state was visible. Beyond that, for about half the shops, it was not.
Nothing about that was careless. That is how most goods reach most Indian shops. The chain was designed to push packets out, as widely and as cheaply as possible. It was never designed to pull them back.
This is not only a food problem. A pipe maker sells through dealers. A pharma distributor sells through chemists. A garment unit sells through agents in five states. In each case, the company knows its first customer well and its last customer barely at all.
I want you to remember that sentence. A chain designed to push cannot pull.

## [09:40] Mechanism three: the test record

The third mechanism is the test record. This is how a food company catches an error before it reaches the customer.
Nestlé said it tested about a thousand batches in its own accredited laboratory. It sent samples from about six hundred batches to an outside laboratory. Together, it said, they covered about a hundred and twenty-five million packets. And all were within the limits.
That is a large body of evidence. Most companies of any size would be glad to have it.
So the fourth question, how are errors caught, has an answer too. There was a check. There were records of the check.
But here is the turn in the story. The regulator was not asking about Nestlé's tests. It was asking about its own.

## [10:30] A line on the pack is a promise

There is one more record in this story that is easy to miss. The words printed on the pack.
The pack said no added MSG. The company said that was true, because it did not add MSG. The regulator read it differently, because the tests showed glutamate, which Nestlé said came naturally from the ingredients.
Whatever the chemistry, here is the systems point. Every claim you make to a customer is a record too. A promise on a quotation. A delivery date on an order. A line on a test certificate. If you cannot defend it with evidence, in the customer's terms, it turns against you on the worst day.
After the crisis, Nestlé took that line off the pack.

## [11:20] The question from outside

The regulator's findings were about specific samples, tested in specific labs. Its order said three things. That lead was above the permitted limit of two and a half parts per million. That the line on the pack, no added MSG, was misleading. And that one variant, the oats masala noodles, had been sold without the required approval.
Nestlé disagreed on the science. It said the regulator had tested the parts of the product separately, rather than the noodles as they are eaten. It said it did not add MSG, and that glutamate occurs naturally in ingredients like groundnut protein, onion and wheat flour.
I am not going to tell you who was right on the chemistry. A court and several laboratories did that work, and we will come to them.
What I want you to see is the shape of the gap. The company had many records. They answered the company's own question, in its own method, in labs it chose. The outside question was different. It was about a sample the company did not pick, tested a way the company did not choose, and about one sentence printed on its own pack.
The records that would settle that question, on the same day, in a form the outsider would accept, did not exist.
The man who took over Nestlé India that summer, Suresh Narayanan, later described the ban as the result of a major breakdown in communication with the government. That is his reading, and I think it is an honest one.

## [13:05] Mechanism four: the feedback loop

The fourth mechanism is the feedback loop. Who finds out when something slips, and how fast?
Let me walk you through the dates, because they tell the whole story.
March 2014. Food safety officers in Barabanki, in Uttar Pradesh, pick up Maggi samples in a routine check.
April 2014. The state laboratory in Gorakhpur reports a problem with the no added MSG line on the label. Nestlé appeals.
The sample is sent for a second test to the Central Food Laboratory in Kolkata. That report is dated the seventh of April, 2015. It says the sample has seventeen point two parts per million of lead, against a limit of two and a half.
Thirtieth of April, 2015. The authorities in Lucknow ask Nestlé to recall that batch.
May. The news breaks. Within days it is everywhere.
So, from the sample to the recall order, the loop took about thirteen months. It ran through a sample bag, a laboratory, an appeal and the post. And by the time the answer came back, the batch had passed its best-before date months earlier.
Nestlé argued that the Kolkata result was high because the sample had been left open for a long time before it was tested. The regulator disputed that. Again, I am not the judge of it. But notice what both sides were arguing about. Not the noodles in the shops. The handling of one sample, over thirteen months. The record of what happened to the sample became as important as the sample itself.
Then the public loop started. That one ran in days.
The third question of the series is about exactly this. A slow loop inside, and a fast loop outside, is the most dangerous combination a business can have. You find out last.

## [15:10] Mechanism five: when the top person is not in the room

The fifth question is the one I ask every owner. What happens when you are not there?
For a company this size, the question becomes: does the system depend on one senior person, or does it run as a process?
Two things in this story suggest the second.
First, the recall itself. Nestlé announced the withdrawal on the fifth of June. By its own account, the recall was fully running two days later. About fifty people in the supply chain team worked on it full time. And the rest of the company kept supplying its other brands as normal.
Think about who actually ran that recall. Not the people in the news. Distributors who took back stock. Shopkeepers who handed over packets and waited for their credit. Truck drivers. Kiln operators. None of them could phone the head of the company for every decision. They needed a process, and they had one.
Second, the way quality is wired. Nestlé has described a structure in which the technical director reports to the head of Nestlé India on a dotted line, and has a straight line to the head office in Switzerland. The point is simple. No country head, however senior, can trade quality for a sales target.
And the top person did change. A new head of Nestlé India took over in the middle of the crisis. The recall did not stop for that.
So the fifth question has a mixed answer. The recall did not depend on one person. But the relationship with the regulator, by the company's own later account, had not been built into the system at all.

## [17:00] What the system looked like on the eve of the crisis

Let me put the five pieces side by side.
The work had a home on every pack. Strong.
The chain could see up to the distributor. Beyond that, for about half the shops, it could not. Weak at the edge.
The test records were large. But they answered the company's question, not the regulator's. A gap.
The feedback loop from the shop shelf back to the company took thirteen months. Slow.
The recall ran as a process, not on one person. Strong.
None of this is unusual. Most good businesses look like this. Strong at the centre. Weaker at the edges. And slow to hear from the edges. If you drew the same five boxes for your own business tonight, I suspect many of you would shade the same two.
Now watch what happens when all five are tested at once.

## [18:00] Act 3: The test

Now the sixth question. What happened when it broke?
The test began on the fifth of June, 2015.
Delhi had already reported that ten of thirteen samples of the seasoning mix were above the lead limit, and banned sales for fifteen days. Gujarat reported twenty-seven of thirty-nine samples and banned sales for thirty days. Other states followed.
That day, Nestlé said it would take Maggi off the shelves. In its own words, it did so "despite the product being safe". The same day, the national food regulator ordered all nine variants withdrawn and recalled.

## [18:30] Pulling a country's worth of noodles back

Nestlé's first estimate was twenty-seven thousand, four hundred and twenty tonnes.
About forty percent of that was no longer in cartons. It was loose packets, on shop shelves and in people's homes. To bring them back, Nestlé had to buy about one point four million cartons from across the country.
To carry all of it in one load would take about two thousand five hundred trucks. But nothing moves in one load. Stock moves from shop to distributor, from distributor to depot, from depot to the point of destruction. Many thousands of truck journeys.
At every step, money changes hands in reverse. Credit notes. Refunds. Cash. Each one has to be recorded, or someone is short at the end of the month.
The noodles were burnt as fuel in five cement kilns. Together, those kilns could take about seven hundred tonnes a day. That alone meant at least forty days of burning.

## [19:35] The number that grew

Here is the figure I find most telling.
The first estimate was about twenty-seven thousand tonnes. By the first of September, by Nestlé's own account to the Supreme Court, about thirty-eight thousand tonnes had been destroyed. And in 2016 the Court allowed Nestlé to destroy a further five hundred and fifty tonnes of expired stock.
I do not read that gap as a failure of honesty. The sources do not say why the figure grew, and some of it may be stock held in the company's own depots. But the point stands. With a chain this wide, you find out how much is out there only when it comes back.
That is the second lesson of this episode in one number. You cannot recall what you cannot trace.

## [20:20] The cost

Nestlé India valued the stock in the market at about two hundred and ten crore rupees. The stock and materials in its own factories and depots, at about a hundred and ten crore more. That was before the cost of collecting, carrying and burning it.
For the quarter from April to June 2015, Nestlé India reported a net loss of about sixty-four crore rupees. A year earlier, in the same quarter, it had made a profit of about two hundred and eighty-eight crore. Most reports said it was the company's first quarterly loss in at least fifteen years.
And the share. For five months, a brand that had held most of its market sold nothing at all.

## [21:10] What the court found

On the thirteenth of August, 2015, the Bombay High Court set aside the national ban.
I want to be exact about what it found, because this part is often told wrongly.
The court held that the order had been passed without a fair hearing, and that the samples had been tested in laboratories that were not accredited by the national accreditation board. It did not declare the noodles safe. It ordered new tests. Five samples of every variant, at three accredited laboratories, in Punjab, Hyderabad and Jaipur, within six weeks. No manufacture and no sale until then.
All ninety samples cleared. New batches from three factories were tested and cleared. On the ninth of November, 2015, Maggi came back, first in about a hundred towns. An online sale of sixty thousand packs sold out in about five minutes. By the thirtieth of November, all five factories were running again.
From ban to shelf. Five months.

## [22:15] The rebuild

The way back came in steps. Press reports of Nielsen data put Maggi at forty-two percent in January 2016. Nestlé itself put it at about fifty-seven in June. Its annual report for 2016 said about sixty. By 2018, the company said a little over sixty. India is now the largest market for Maggi in the world.
And the company changed things. It took the no added MSG line off the pack. It said it would run a round-the-clock consumer helpline. It said it would work with rival companies to help build the government's testing capacity, with laboratories and training. It said it would rebuild its ties with the owners of almost four million shops.
The rebuild was not a return to the old system. It was a chance to build a better one.

## [23:05] Act 4: What this means for a business of 15 to 100 people

Let me bring this back to your business. Four lessons. Each one comes from a moment in the story.
The first lesson. A batch record is a home for work.
When the authorities in Lucknow asked about one batch, Nestlé could say when it was made, how many packs it held, and when it expired. That is the record doing its job.
In your business, what is the batch? If you make parts, it is the lot. If you trade, it is the consignment. If you run a CA practice or a consultancy, it is the client file and the version of the working you sent.
Each one needs a home. A number. A date. A name against it. And the next step. If the only record of which customer got which lot is in the dispatch man's head, the work does not have a home. It has a tenant.
One more thing. The record has to be made at the moment the work happens. Not at the end of the week, from memory. A batch record written up on Saturday is a story, not a record.

## [24:25] Lesson two: you cannot recall what you cannot trace

The second lesson. You cannot recall what you cannot trace.
Nestlé could see every carton up to its distributors. Beyond that, for about half the shops, it could not. And the amount it destroyed ended about ten thousand tonnes above its first estimate.
Ask yourself one plain question this week. If a supplier told you that one lot of raw material was faulty, could you list every order it went into, and every customer who received those orders, by this evening?
For many owners the honest answer is, I would have to ask three people and wait two days. That is not a discipline problem. It is a design problem. The sheet that records the lot at the gate also has to record where it went at dispatch. One column. Filled in every time.

## [25:20] Lesson three: answer the outside question the same day

The third lesson. The system has to be able to answer a question from outside on the same day.
Nestlé had large numbers of test records. But the outside question came in a different shape. Different samples, different labs, one line on the pack. It took a court and five months to settle.
Your outside questions are smaller, but they come. A large customer runs a supplier audit. A bank asks for stock statements and debtor ageing before renewal. A GST notice asks about one invoice from two years ago. A client asks who approved a figure in last year's return.
The question is never, do you have the information somewhere. The question is, can you produce it today, in the form they asked for, without the owner sitting up till midnight.
Here is a test you can run this Friday. Pick one order from last month, at random. Ask your team where every part of it came from, and where every part of it went. If it is minutes, you have a system. If it is days, you have people who are good at remembering.
In my family's firm, when a lender asks a question, the answer comes from the sheet. Not from someone remembering. That is the only reason we can answer it the same day.

## [26:50] Lesson four: records, not memory, and a better rebuild

The fourth lesson has two halves.
A crisis is answered by records, not by memory. In June 2015, a brand with thirty years of goodwill could not stay on the shelf on the strength of that goodwill. The shelf came back only when ninety samples, tested in labs the court chose, came back clear. Goodwill buys you patience. Records buy you the answer.
And the rebuild is a chance to make the system better than it was. Nestlé took a line off its pack that it could not defend in the regulator's terms. It said it would put a helpline in place. It offered to help build testing capacity outside its own walls.
In a smaller firm, the bad month is the moment the team will accept a change they would have resisted in a good one. A lost customer. A wrong dispatch. A missed filing date. That is the week to give the work a home, not the week to find someone to blame.
People at Nestlé have said they learned more in those five months than in the years before. The question is whether the learning is written into the system, or only into the memory of the people who lived through it. Memory leaves when they do.
[your own line]

## [28:20] Close

Maggi took two minutes to cook and five months to come back. The two minutes were the product. The five months were the system being tested.
So here are the six answers, in one breath. The work lived on the pack and in the batch record. Its state was visible up to the distributor, and not beyond. The feedback loop inside took thirteen months. Errors were checked by a large body of tests, but in the company's own terms. The recall did not depend on one person. And when it broke, the brand came back in five months, and came back changed.
None of that needed a hero. It needed records that existed before the bad day, and people who knew where to find them.
This is the work I do now. In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, I designed one place where every piece of work lives, with a name, a date and a next step, so that the answer to a hard question is on the sheet and not in someone's head. Now I set up the same kind of system for owners of businesses with fifteen to a hundred people, one process at a time.
Start with one question. If something went wrong with one order today, could you trace it by the evening?
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.

## [29:55] End card

Thank you for watching. Next week, another business, another system.
