script:
## [00:00] Six in the morning, a village in Anand district

It is a little after six in the morning, in a village in Anand district, in Gujarat. A woman walks to a small room at the end of the lane. She carries a steel can. There are four people ahead of her. Nobody pushes.
At the window, the secretary pours her milk into a measure. The weight shows on a small screen. A little milk goes into a machine. Within a minute, a slip prints. It shows the date, the shift, her member number, the litres, the fat, the rate and the amount.
She reads it. She folds it. She goes home.
Nobody argued. Nobody phoned anyone. Nobody senior was in the room. This evening she will come back and do it again. So will about 36 lakh other farmers, in about 18,600 villages across Gujarat.
This scene is a composite. I have put it together from the dairy board's own handbook for collection staff. But some version of it happens twice a day, every day.

## [01:10] The question

I wanted to understand that room. Because it does something most of our businesses cannot do. It settles a payment, fairly, with lakhs of people, every day, without the owner standing there.
So the question for this episode is simple. How does a business owned by lakhs of small farmers pay every one of them correctly, on a day they know, without anyone having to remember, argue or chase?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [01:45] Your desk, this morning

Let me start with a desk I know.
A supplier calls at ten. He wants to know when his payment will come. You are not sure. Accounts knows, or thinks it knows. You call accounts. Accounts calls you back at twelve.
At two, a worker says the rate on his slip is wrong. He may be right. He may not be. Either way, it comes to you, because you are the only person both sides will believe.
At five, a customer says the last lot was short. Was it checked before it left? Somebody says yes. Nobody can show it.
None of this is a big problem. Each one takes five minutes. But each one needs you. By the evening, you have been the accounts desk, the quality check and the referee. Everything has come through you.
I saw this in my family's firm, VSP Consultants, before we changed how the work was held. The owner is not slow. The owner is simply the only place where the answer lives.
Now let me take you somewhere the same three questions come up lakhs of times a day. And almost none of them reach the top.

## [03:05] Kaira, 1946: a price set by someone else

Go back to Kaira district, in central Gujarat, in the 1940s.
The farmers here kept buffaloes. Their milk went to Bombay under a government milk scheme. The scheme bought from a private dairy at Anand called Polson, which held the right to collect milk across the district. Between Polson and the villages stood the milk contractors.
The union's own history puts it plainly. Nobody had fixed the price paid to the farmer. The contractor fixed it. The farmer sold at that price, or did not sell at all.
That is the position of every small supplier with one buyer. The price is a favour. So is the payment day.
The farmers went to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. He gave them specific advice. Form your own cooperative. Own your own processing. Ask the government to buy from you. If it refuses, stop selling to the middlemen, and accept the loss for a while.
On the fourth of January 1946, at a meeting in Samarkha village, the farmers resolved to do exactly that. The government refused. So the farmers stopped selling milk, for fifteen days. Bombay's milk scheme nearly collapsed. The Milk Commissioner came to Anand and accepted their demand.
On the fourteenth of December 1946, the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union was registered. Its chairman was Tribhuvandas Patel, a Gandhian and a freedom fighter from Anand.

## [04:35] The real problem was trust

The strike won the farmers a buyer. It did not yet solve the harder problem.
Think about the transaction itself. A farmer with two buffaloes brings a few litres. Someone has to measure it, judge its quality, write it down, and pay for it, on some day.
At every one of those steps, a person with more power can cheat a person with less. A thumb on the scale. A low reading. A missing entry. A payment that comes late, or not at all. Under the contractors, each step depended on trusting one man.
Tribhuvandas Patel insisted on two rules from the start. Every village society was open to every milk producer, regardless of caste, creed or community. And every member had one vote, whatever his wealth. The union's own account records both.
Those rules settled who belonged. The next question was harder. How could a small room in each village treat everyone the same, twice a day, with nobody from Anand watching?
In May 1949, a young engineer arrived in Anand to serve out a government bond at the creamery. His name was Verghese Kurien. In his autobiography, I Too Had a Dream, he called the town "excruciatingly unexciting and conservative." He meant to leave as soon as he could. Tribhuvandas Patel asked him to stay a little and help set up the union's equipment.
He stayed for the rest of his working life. But notice the order. The farmers built the union first.

## [06:20] Five things the counter does

Here is what I noticed when I read the handbook that India's National Dairy Development Board gives to milk procurement staff. It describes the village counter in plain steps. There is no slogan in it.
There are five mechanisms. A fixed rhythm. A test done in front of the person. A record the farmer carries home. A payment on a known day. And one rule, the same in every village.
Let me take them one at a time.

## [06:55] One: a fixed rhythm, twice a day

The first mechanism is the rhythm.
Every morning and every evening, members bring their milk to the society at set times. The handbook lists collection twice a day as the society's first function. The truck from the union arrives on the society's fixed schedule, picks up the milk, and leaves. If you are late, the milk misses the truck.
This rhythm was not a management idea. Milk forced it. Milk spoils. Buffaloes are milked morning and evening. So the business had to move twice a day, every day, through festivals, and through the days when the secretary has a fever.
But look at what the rhythm does for management. Nobody needs to be reminded to bring milk. Nobody needs to ask the driver when he is coming. Nobody needs to ask whether collection is open today. The time itself is the instruction.
In June 1948, the union was pasteurising about 250 litres a day from two village societies. By the end of that year, 432 farmers had joined, and the union handled 5,000 litres a day. That growth did not need more supervision. It needed more people arriving at the same two times.
In most of our firms, the rhythm is the owner. Dispatch happens when he asks. The review happens when he remembers. Payment happens when someone chases. Take the owner away, and the rhythm stops.
At the village counter, the rhythm belongs to the day, not to a person.

## [08:35] Two: the test, in front of the farmer

The second mechanism is the test.
Milk is paid for by its quality, and for most of Amul's history, quality meant fat. A litre with more fat is worth more. So the fat reading is the money.
The old method was called the Gerber test. You put sulphuric acid into a thin glass tube called a butyrometer. You add a measured amount of milk, then a little amyl alcohol. You seal it, shake it, spin it in a centrifuge for five minutes, and read the fat off a scale on the glass. It works. But it is slow, it uses acid, and at a busy counter with a few hundred members, it takes time.
So the dairy board worked with a Danish manufacturer on a small electronic tester for village use. It reads fat from the way light scatters through milk, and shows the number on a display. Today, many societies use an automatic milk collection unit. The weighing scale and the milk analyser are joined to a small computer. The member's number goes in. The machines capture the weight and the fat. The rate comes from a chart the union sends. The slip prints.
In the older counters, the result itself rode on the rhythm. The handbook describes the truck crew bringing back the fat slip of the previous shift, along with the clean cans. The answer arrived on schedule, with the truck, not when someone remembered to send it.
Here is the detail I find most important. The handbook says test results are recorded against a sample number, not a name, so the tester does not know whose milk he is testing. And if a member doubts a reading, she can ask for a retest before the samples are thrown away.
The handbook also notes what happened when electronic testers and collection units arrived. Member participation and trust grew.
Think about why. The test is fair, yes. But more than that, it is seen to be fair, by the person whose money depends on it, at the moment it happens. There is nothing to argue about later, because nothing was decided out of sight.

## [11:00] Three: the record the farmer carries home

The third mechanism is the record.
Every pour is written in two places. Once in the society's purchase register. And once in the member's own card or passbook, which she keeps. Where the counter is computerised, she also gets the printed slip. Date. Morning or evening. Cow or buffalo. Her member number. Weight. Fat. Rate. Amount.
So the work lives in a place both sides can see. Not in the secretary's memory. Not in a diary in a drawer. On a piece of paper in the farmer's hand, and in a register the auditor will check.
The newer systems go further. A dairy board presentation on collection software describes a digital passbook and a text-message service, so a farmer can check her quantity, her quality, today's price and her balance due, without asking anyone.
This is the first of my six questions. Where does the work live? Here, it lives on the slip and in the passbook.
It also answers the second question. How can anyone see the state of the work? The farmer sees it before she leaves the window. Litres, fat, rate, amount. If something is wrong, she knows in a minute, not at the end of the month.
Compare that with a supplier in your city waiting for his payment. He does not know what you have recorded against his name. He finds out when the money arrives, or does not. So he calls. And the call comes to you.

## [12:40] Four: payment on a known day

The fourth mechanism is the payment day.
I want to be exact here, because this part is often told loosely. The payment cycle at a village society is not the same everywhere, and it has changed over time.
The dairy board's handbook says a society pays its members daily, weekly or every ten days, as its elected managing committee decides. The same handbook says the union pays each society through the bank at a regular interval, weekly or every ten days. That interval is generally not changed, and it is the same for all societies. A government note in 2016 described the sector's cycles as weekly and ten-day. And in 2021, the managing director of the Kaira union wrote that each society is paid once in ten days.
So the cycle varies. What does not vary is that it is fixed, and known in advance.
The price is fixed in the same way. It is set per kilogram of fat, from the union's chart, not by the secretary. The federation reported paying 337 rupees per kilogram of fat in 2009 to 2010, and 765 rupees in 2019 to 2020. The farmer does not negotiate that number at the window. She checks it.
Since the end of 2016, payments have also moved into farmers' bank accounts.
At the end of the year, there is one more payment. Part of the society's surplus goes back to members as a bonus, in proportion to the milk each one supplied.
That is the third of my six questions. What is the feedback loop? Here, it runs on a timetable. Every shift, the slip. Every cycle, the money. Every month, the committee meets. Every year, the bonus and the audit.
A farmer does not need to ask when she will be paid. A secretary does not need to decide when to pay. A chairman does not need to approve each payment. The calendar decides.

## [14:55] Five: one rule, the same in every village

The fifth mechanism is the structure, and it is simpler than it sounds.
At the bottom is the village society, owned by its members. In the middle is the district union, owned by the societies. At the top is the state federation, formed by the unions. In Gujarat, that federation is GCMMF, set up in 1973, which sells under the Amul brand. Members elect the leaders at each level. Professional managers answer to those leaders.
Each tier does only what it is best placed to do. The village receives, tests, records and pays. The union buys all of the societies' milk, processes it, and supplies feed, vets and breeding services. The federation sells, under one name.
This answers my fourth question. How are errors caught before they travel? At the society, after each shift, the whole collection is sampled and tested again as one, which the handbook calls the general test. At the union, the milk is tested again at the dock. An auditor checks that every member has a passbook and that every pour is entered.
And since the 1990s, the Kaira union has chilled milk at the society itself, below four degrees within one to two hours of milking, so quality does not slip on the road. By 2016 to 2017, it had a bulk milk cooler in every one of its 1,202 village societies. Its tankers now carry sealed automatic samplers, so each society's sample is drawn by a machine, not a hand.
And it answers my fifth question. What happens when the owner is away? At the village counter, there is no owner. The committee is elected and unpaid. The secretary is paid to run the counter. The rate chart comes from the union. The rule is the same in Anand as in a village two hundred kilometres away. Nobody needs to be present for it to be kept.

## [17:05] What the counter does not need

Notice what the counter does not need.
It does not need the chairman to approve each payment. It does not need a call from Anand to open on time. It does not need the secretary to be a good judge of character, or the farmer to trust him personally. It does not need anyone to remember who brought what last Tuesday.
All of that has been moved out of people's heads, and into the rhythm, the test, the slip and the cycle. What is left for people is the work itself. Pouring, testing, loading, paying.
That is the difference between a system and a set of good people. Good people get tired. They go on leave. They leave. A rhythm does not.
Even the best-known person in this story eventually left, and not happily. I will come to that. The counters did not notice. They opened the next morning, at the same time.

## [18:05] Every system meets a bad year

Every system looks good on a normal Tuesday. The real question is what happens when something breaks. A flood of supply. A collapse in demand. A crisis nobody planned for.
Amul has been tested more than once. I want to show you three tests. The first, in the 1950s, was too much milk. The second, from 1970, was scale, whether the counter could be copied across India. The third was March 2020.

## [18:35] Test one: the winter surplus

Buffaloes give about two and a half times as much milk in winter as in summer. By 1953, the Bombay scheme could not take the extra winter milk. Farmers were once again selling their surplus to middlemen, at low rates.
This mattered for the whole design. The farmer pours twice a day because the society will take all of her milk. If the society cannot take it in winter, the rhythm breaks, and the contractors come back.
The union's answer was a factory. A plant to turn surplus milk into milk powder and butter, costing about fifty lakh rupees. President Rajendra Prasad laid its foundation stone in November 1954. Prime Minister Nehru opened it on the thirty-first of October 1955. The union describes it as the first plant to make these products from buffalo milk at commercial scale.
The lesson is quiet, but important. When the promise at the counter came under pressure, they did not change the counter. They built capacity behind it, so the promise could hold.

## [19:45] Test two: copying the counter across India

The second test was scale.
On the thirty-first of October 1964, Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri came to Anand to open the union's cattle feed plant. He spent a night with farmers in the district. Then he asked Kurien to repeat the Anand model across the country. The National Dairy Development Board was set up at Anand in 1965. Operation Flood began in 1970.
What travelled was not a brand. It was the counter. A village society, a district union, a state federation, and the same routine at the bottom. Collect twice a day. Test. Record. Pay.
By the end of the first phase, in 1981, the programme had formed 13,270 village dairy cooperatives, covering about seventeen and a half lakh farm families. By the end of the third phase, the count was 72,744 cooperatives and about 93 lakh families. Those are the dairy board's own figures.
A rule that only works because one good person is watching cannot be copied seventy-two thousand times. A rule that is the same at every counter can.

## [21:00] Test three: March 2020

The third test is the one I find most striking.
India's lockdown began on the twenty-fifth of March 2020. For three days, Amul's sales rose as people stocked up. On the fourth day, they fell by about thirty percent. Hotels, sweet shops and restaurants shut. Many smaller and private dairies stopped buying milk.
Think about what that means at the village counter. A farmer still has buffaloes to milk, twice a day. If nobody buys, the milk is lost, and so is the month's income.
Amul did not stop collecting. Its managing director said in April 2020 that it was taking ten to fifteen percent more milk than usual, because the smaller dairies had closed. He said it was still paying forty-two rupees a litre for buffalo milk at six percent fat, and thirty-one rupees for cow milk at three and a half percent fat. The extra milk went into butter and milk powder, which keep for a year or two.
At its annual meeting that July, the federation said the Gujarat unions had procured an additional 35 lakh litres a day during the lockdown, giving about 800 crore rupees extra to rural milk producers. In June, the managing director said Amul had put about 9,000 crore rupees into the rural economy, in Gujarat and the other states where it works.
Why could it do this? Not only because people made brave decisions in a boardroom, though they did. It was because the counter already worked on a rhythm everyone knew. The society takes the milk. The test is done in front of you. The rate comes from the chart. The money comes on the known day. Nothing about that had to be invented in a crisis. It only had to keep going.

## [22:55] What the test showed

So, my sixth question. What happened when it broke? Demand broke. The counter did not. Morning and evening, the windows opened, the milk was tested, the slips printed, and the payments followed on the cycle.

## [23:10] Where the comparison stops

Before I draw lessons, let me be honest about the limits.
Amul is not a forty-person firm. It is a federation of cooperatives, owned by its own suppliers. In its early years, the state bought its milk on contract at stable prices. Operation Flood was funded with donated milk powder and World Bank loans. Its boards are elected, and like many cooperatives in India, it has a political life. Chairmanships have been contested. Kurien himself resigned as chairman of the federation in March 2006, ahead of a no-confidence motion by his own board. Operation Flood also had serious critics, who questioned who gained most from it.
And yet the counters kept opening after 2006, morning and evening, as before.
You cannot copy a federation. You should not try.
But you can copy the counter. Because the counter is the place where your business meets a supplier, a worker or a customer. And that moment either needs you, or it does not.
Here are four things I take from Anand.

## [24:20] Lesson one: a fixed rhythm removes the need to chase

First. A fixed rhythm removes the need to chase.
The farmer does not ask when collection opens. It opens at the same time every day.
In your firm, pick the one thing you chase most. For many owners, it is dispatch. Give it a time. Dispatch closes at four. Whatever is packed, checked and billed by four goes today. Whatever is not goes tomorrow, and the sheet shows why. Then give the week a rhythm. On Monday, everyone gets their list. On Friday, everyone sees their score.
Once the time is fixed, you stop being the alarm clock. You no longer walk to the floor at six in the evening to ask, "ho gaya?" Four o'clock has already answered.

## [25:10] Lesson two: a test done in front of the person removes the argument

Second. A test done in front of the person removes the argument.
At the counter, the farmer watches her milk being tested. If she doubts it, she asks for a retest, there and then. Nobody argues a week later.
Most disputes in our firms come from a check done out of sight. The customer says the lot was short. The supervisor says it was full. Nobody can show it. So move the check to where both sides can see it. Weigh the lot with the driver present, and photograph the reading. Read the quote back to the client on the call, line by line, before you send it. Count the stock with the store keeper and the accountant together, on a fixed date each month.
The aim is not to catch anyone. The aim is to settle the question at the moment it is cheapest to settle.

## [26:10] Lesson three: a visible record settles the payment

Third. A visible record settles the payment.
The farmer leaves with a slip. Litres, fat, rate, amount. When the money comes, she checks it against her own record.
Think of your suppliers, your contract workers, your clients. What do they hold in their hand after each transaction? Usually nothing. So they call. A simple record, shared at the moment of the work, changes that. A delivery note signed by both sides. A job card that shows the hours. A client file where the client can see what stage the work is at, and what is due from them.
When both sides hold the same record, the payment stops being a negotiation. It becomes a check.

## [27:00] Lesson four: the same rule at the smallest unit

Fourth. The system grows because the rule at the smallest unit is the same everywhere.
Operation Flood did not copy Kurien. It copied the counter, more than seventy thousand times.
In a firm of forty, the smallest unit is one piece of work. One order. One quote. One client file. If each of those has a home, with a name, a date and a next step, then it does not matter whether the owner is at the desk, at a wedding, or on a plane. The rule holds.
So do not start with the whole firm. Start with one process. Make the rule at that counter the same every time. Run it for a month. Then copy it to the next process, and the next branch, without changing the rule.
That is how a small room in Samarkha became more than seventy thousand rooms across India. Not by finding seventy thousand remarkable people. By keeping one rule simple enough to repeat.

## [28:05] What I do now

In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, we were the follow-up department for years. Every update, every payment question, every "is it done" came to one desk. What changed it was not working harder. It was giving the work a home, a fixed rhythm, and a record everyone could see. [your own line]
This is the work I do now, at Venture Drafters. I sit with an owner, find the one process that comes through them most often, and design its counter: the rhythm, the check and the record. We set it up on your own sheet, train your team, and manage it with you.
Four things, then. A fixed rhythm, so nobody has to chase. A check done in front of the person, so nobody has to argue. A record both sides can see, so the payment settles itself. And one rule, the same at the smallest counter, so the firm can grow without the owner in every room.
A farmer in Anand does not need to chase her payment. Your supplier should not need to either. And neither should you.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.

This was Built to Run. Every figure in this episode, and its source, is listed in the description. Thank you for watching.

script:
## [0:00] Cold open: two tables

It is a weekday morning in Madurai, in Tamil Nadu. In an operating theatre, a surgeon sits on a stool between two operating tables.
On the left table, she is removing a clouded lens from a patient's eye and placing a new one. On the right table, a second patient is already lying still. Cleaned. Numbed. Covered. The lens for that eye is already on the tray.
She finishes on the left. She turns her stool to the right. She begins again.
Behind her, a team takes the first patient out and brings the next one in. Nobody asks her what to do next. Nobody hands her a file and waits for a decision. The next patient is simply there, ready, when she turns.
The operation itself takes a few minutes. Everything around those minutes has been done by someone else, the same way, every time.

## [1:00] The question

This is Aravind Eye Care System. In the year that ended in March 2026, its hospitals and clinics handled more than 67 lakh outpatient visits. They performed more than 8 lakh surgeries, laser procedures and injections. About half of those operations were free or steeply subsidised. And the organisation pays its own way.
Today's question is simple. How do you design a business so that the most expensive hour in it is spent only on the work that truly needs that person?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [1:35] Act 1: The owner's problem

Let me start with a desk I know well.
The owner of a 40-person firm in Indore comes in at ten. By eleven he has checked three quotes, approved one dispatch, taken two client calls and answered a question about a payment that was due last week. By lunch he has not yet done the one thing only he can do. Perhaps it is pricing a large order. Perhaps it is meeting the banker. Perhaps it is thinking about next year.
He is the most expensive person in the business. And his hour is going on work that costs a few hundred rupees.
He is not lazy. He is not disorganised. He works harder than anyone in the building. The problem is that the work has no other home. If he does not check, nobody checks. If he does not chase, nobody chases. He is the memory, the follow-up department and the feedback loop.
Fifty years ago, an eye surgeon in Madurai faced the same arithmetic. Only his numbers were much larger, and the cost of getting it wrong was blindness.

## [2:55] A retired surgeon starts again

His name was Dr Govindappa Venkataswamy. Everyone called him Dr V.
He was born in 1918. He served as an army doctor, and in 1948 he was discharged after developing rheumatoid arthritis. He spent more than a year in bed. He went on to become an eye surgeon anyway, and spent his working life in government service.
In 1976 he retired. He was 58. Most people would have stopped there.
He did not. With his family and a few colleagues, he opened a hospital in Madurai. It had eleven beds and four doctors. Aravind's own history records exactly that: eleven beds, four medical officers.
This year, 2026, is Aravind's fiftieth.
I want you to hold that picture for a moment. A man past retirement age, eleven beds, a family business in the plainest sense. That is closer to the firms watching this than to any large hospital chain.

## [4:00] The size of the problem

Here is what he was up against.
In the 1980s, cataract caused about 80 percent of the blindness in India. That figure comes from a paper Aravind's own leaders wrote in 2008. A cataract is a clouding of the lens inside the eye. It comes with age. Left alone, it takes a person's sight.
The cure is a short operation. Remove the clouded lens. Put in a clear artificial one. It is one of the most reliable operations in medicine.
So the problem was never the operation. The problem was the hours. There were only so many eye surgeons. And each surgeon's day was full of work that was not surgery. Examining patients. Measuring eyes. Explaining. Writing notes. Waiting for the next patient to be ready. Waiting for instruments.
If a surgeon does everything, a surgeon does a few operations a day. Multiply that across a country, and millions of people wait in the dark for a queue that never moves.
Dr V's question was not, how do I make my surgeons work harder. It was, which minutes of this whole process truly need a surgeon?

## [5:15] Your version of the question

I want you to ask the same question about your own business before we go further.
Take your most important process. A quote. An order. A dispatch. A client file. Now ask: of all the steps in it, which ones truly need you? Not which ones you usually do. Which ones need you.
For most owners I speak to, the honest answer is one or two steps. Pricing. A final judgement. A relationship. The rest, they do because there is nobody else who knows how, and nowhere else for the work to wait.
Hold your list in your head. We will come back to it at the end. Now let us look at how Aravind answered the question.

## [6:00] Act 2: The system

Aravind's answer has five parts. I will take them one at a time. The surgeon's minutes. A trained person for every other step. The path to the door and back again. The score. And the lens.
As we go, I will keep asking the same questions I ask of every business in this series. Where does the work live? How can anyone see its state? Who finds out when something slips? How are mistakes caught? And what happens when the founder is not in the room?

## [6:35] Mechanism one: the surgeon's minutes

Start in the operating theatre, where we began.
Each surgeon works with two operating tables. While the surgeon operates on one patient, the next patient is being prepared on the other. Aravind's leaders described this in a 2008 paper in Community Eye Health. They call it a planned daily schedule, with equipment and support staff matched to the surgeon's pace, and supplies checked before the list begins.
Under that set-up, one surgeon completes six to eight operations an hour.
A University of Michigan health economist, David Hutton, presented figures in 2014 that put an average cataract operation at Aravind at about six minutes. The same operation in the United States averaged about 21 minutes. At Aravind there were four nurses in each theatre, and two patients in the room at once.
Think about what that means. The surgeon never waits. Not for a patient. Not for an instrument. Not for a decision. The instruments for each operation come on a standard tray, laid out the same way every time, so the surgeon's hand goes to the same place without looking. The patient arrives already prepared, by someone trained to prepare them.
So where does the work live? It does not live in the surgeon's memory. It lives in the sequence. In the schedule for the day. On the tray. On the second table.

## [8:10] What that does to a surgeon's year

Now add those minutes up over a year.
In 2011 the American broadcaster NPR reported that Aravind's surgeons averaged about 2,000 operations a year. The average for an eye surgeon in the United States was about 125. Thulasiraj Ravilla, Aravind's director of operations, told NPR that compared with an average surgeon in India, Aravind's surgeons were probably four or five times as productive.
I want to be careful here. The first two figures are NPR's own reporting. I could not trace them to a published audit. The comparison with India is Aravind's own estimate. But the direction is not in doubt, and the reason is not that Aravind's surgeons are superhuman.
The reason is design. Dr V loved to talk about how American chains delivered the same thing, reliably, at great scale. In an interview filmed for American public television, he put it simply: "In America you have models, whether it is Sears stores or McDonald's hamburgers."
People sometimes laugh at that comparison. A hospital is not a burger shop. But he was not talking about food. He was talking about a sequence designed so that every step is known in advance, every step has a trained person, and the result does not depend on who is on shift that day.

## [9:35] Mechanism two: a trained person for every other step

If the surgeon only does the surgical minutes, someone else must do everything else. At Aravind, that someone is a very particular group of people.
Aravind calls them allied ophthalmic personnel. In the wider field they are called mid-level ophthalmic personnel. Most are young women from rural families, recruited after they finish school and trained by Aravind itself.
According to Aravind's activity report for 2024-25, they make up 64 percent of its whole workforce. Nearly two of every three people.
An Aravind post published by the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness in 2017 describes how they arrive. Each year, about 2,000 young women apply. About 900 are chosen. Most are 17 to 19 years old. They train for two years: about eighteen months of classes Aravind wrote itself, then six months of practice in a hospital.
Then they run the steps that do not need a surgeon. Registration and records. Measuring how well a patient sees. Measuring the power of glasses. Explaining the operation and what comes after. Preparing the patient. Working in the theatre. Caring for the instruments.
Notice what this does. Each step has a name and a person. Each step is done the same way, because it was taught the same way.

## [11:00] The written standard

Here is one small example that tells you the whole idea.
After surgery, every patient is counselled. How to put in the eye drops. When they can bathe. When they can go back to work. What to watch for. Which signs mean they must come back at once.
At Aravind, that counselling follows a written checklist. Aravind's doctors described it in a 2016 paper. The checklist makes sure every point is covered, for every patient, every time.
Now think about who is holding that checklist. Often a young woman in her first year of work. Without the checklist, she would need years of experience to know what to say. With it, she can do it well in her first week.
That is what a standard is for. It is not a cage. It is the thing that lets a new person be good on week one. The knowledge lives on the page, not only in the senior person's head.

## [12:05] Mechanism three: the path to the door, and back again

The third mechanism is about where patients come from, and where they go after.
The people who most need cataract surgery are often the least able to reach a hospital. Elderly. Poor. Far from town. So Aravind does not wait for them.
In the year ending March 2026, Aravind ran 3,450 free eye camps. Those camps screened about five and a half lakh people. And they led to 1,04,589 free operations. Aravind says camps account for about 30 percent of its cataract surgeries.
The second route is the vision centre. It is a small eye clinic in a rural town. A trained technician sees every patient first. Then an ophthalmologist at the base hospital reviews the case by video and prescribes treatment. Aravind reported that its 117 vision centres in 2024-25 covered about one crore twenty lakh people, and could handle about 90 percent of basic eye care close to home. By March 2026 there were 120 centres, with more than 11 lakh visits in the year.
So how can anyone see the state of the work? A patient moves from the camp, to the vision centre or the hospital, to the theatre, to the ward, and back home. Every station records them. Every station is counted. Aravind publishes its patient statistics every month on its own website.

## [13:35] Follow-up has a home

Now the part I find most useful for owners. The way back.
Every patient Aravind operates on is examined on the first day after surgery. Counselling is repeated before they go home. And the visit at one month is not a suggestion. It is a planned step. The patient's glasses are measured. The pressure in the eye is checked. A decision is made about the second eye.
The vision centres help here too. Aravind's 2013-14 report notes that because the clinic is near the patient's home, follow-up for long-term conditions like diabetic eye disease and glaucoma is better.
So who finds out when something slips? Not the surgeon, by remembering. The follow-up is on the schedule, with a day and a place. If a patient does not come back, the gap shows on the list.
Follow-up is a step with a home. It is not a favour that a busy expert remembers to do when there is time.

## [14:40] Mechanism four: the score

The fourth mechanism is the score. Aravind counts its mistakes, and it counts them openly.
In 2012 Aravind's doctors published a study of 79,777 consecutive cataract operations at their Madurai hospital over twelve months. Every complication during surgery was counted, and sorted by who did the operation.
Staff surgeons had a complication rate of 0.79 percent. Fellows, 1.19 percent. Residents in training, 2.06 percent. Visiting trainees, 5 percent.
Then the score changed the standard. Trainees had many more complications with one technique than with another. So the authors recommended that new surgeons learn the safer technique first.
Another example. Infection after eye surgery is rare but serious. Aravind added an antibiotic injection inside the eye at the end of every operation. Its doctors report that infections fell from eight in every 10,000 operations to two.
How does that compare with a rich country? Britain's national cataract audit, covering more than 55,000 operations in NHS hospitals between 2001 and 2006, reported 1.92 percent for its main complication. Aravind's measure is broader and from a different period, so I will not say Aravind is twice as good. The fair statement is that its published rates sit at or below published British figures.
So how are errors caught? They are counted, by person and by type, and the count changes how the work is done.

## [16:15] Mechanism five: the lens

The last mechanism sits outside the hospital.
In the 1980s, an imported artificial lens cost more than 100 US dollars, or more than 3,000 rupees. That one part made modern cataract surgery too expensive for the poor.
So in 1992 Aravind set up its own manufacturer in Madurai, called Aurolab. Its first lenses sold at 270 rupees, about a tenth of the imported price. Today a basic lens costs two to three dollars. Aurolab says it exports to about 160 countries.
A 2021 costing study in NEJM Catalyst, by researchers at Stanford with co-authors from Aravind and Tilganga, compared the cost of the same operation at four sites. If an American hospital department costs 100 dollars, Aravind cost 21 dollars 50 cents, adjusted for local prices. The authors put it down to faster patient flow, more use of trained mid-level staff, and tight control of supplies.
I include the lens for one reason. Dr V did not stop at the hospital wall. He looked at the one input that made every operation expensive, and he redesigned where it came from. Most owners have one input like that. A supplier who is always late. A part that is always short. It is worth asking whether that, too, needs a home.

## [17:35] When the founder is not in the room

Five mechanisms. The surgeon's minutes. A trained person and a written standard for every other step. A path to the door and back. A score that changes the standard. And a lens made at a price the poor can pay.
Notice that none of them needs Dr V in the room. He could only stand in one theatre on any morning. The two tables worked in every theatre.
Which brings us to the real test.

## [18:05] Act 3: The test

Every system looks good while its builder is standing next to it. The test is what happens when the builder is gone, or when the world stops.
Aravind has faced both.

## [18:20] The founder's death

Dr V died on 7 July 2006. He was 87.
In many family firms, that is the year things start to slip. The founder held the relationships, the standards, the memory. When he goes, people find out how much lived in his head.
At Aravind, the work carried on. In 2005, the year before he died, Aravind's five hospitals performed 1,78,939 cataract operations. In 2007, the year after, they performed 1,80,991. The work held steady through the loss. That 2007 figure is about six times the figure for 1988. By the year ending March 2011, the system performed 3,15,483 surgeries and ran 36 vision centres.
The leadership passed to people he had trained and worked beside. Today the chairman is Dr R. D. Ravindran. The director of operations is Thulasiraj Ravilla, the same man who told NPR about surgeon productivity in 2011.
There was a second loss last year. In July 2025, Dr P. Namperumalsamy, one of Aravind's founding members, died at 86. The year that ended in March 2026 was still the largest in Aravind's history.
Why did it hold? Look back at the five mechanisms. The sequence in the theatre was written down. The training school produced a new intake every year. The checklists did not leave when he left. The monthly and yearly counts kept going, so everyone could see whether the work was slipping. He had spent thirty years putting the knowledge somewhere other than his own head.
The founder built the system. The system did not need the founder to keep running it.

## [20:00] The year the doors closed

The harder test came in 2020.
For the first time since 1976, Aravind closed its doors to routine patients. During the lockdown its hospitals saw only emergencies. Free eye camps were suspended for about eight months. Only 440 camps were held in the whole year, about a fifth of the usual number. The vision centres were shut for about two months.
The numbers fell hard. Outpatient visits fell from about 46 lakh in 2019-20 to about 29 lakh in 2020-21. Surgeries fell from 5,19,138 to 3,27,786. Aravind's own report puts the fall at about 38 percent.
What matters is what the system did next. Teleconsultation was set up at every base hospital, so patients with urgent problems could be seen without travelling. A scheduling system was brought in to manage patient flow under the new safety rules. Aravind reported that it cut long waiting times.
Digital payment was linked to the hospital software. Within six months it made up 41 percent of non-credit payments. The vision centres reopened under written safety protocols, and by August 2020 they were fully working. Twelve new vision centres opened during that same difficult year. And Aurolab supplied protective equipment free of cost to other eye hospitals.

## [21:20] The recovery

In 2021-22, surgeries reached 5,24,672. That was above the year before the pandemic. By 2025-26, the figure was 8,02,003 surgeries, laser procedures and injections.
The lesson is not that Aravind was lucky. It is that the work had homes that could be moved. The consultation could move to a screen. The queue could move to a schedule. The payment could move to a phone. Because each step was written down and owned by someone, each step could be changed without the whole system falling over.
Compare that with a business where the work lives in the owner's head. When the owner cannot come in, nothing moves, because nobody else knows what the next step is. At Aravind, in the worst year in its history, people knew the next step. They were simply asked to take it in a different way.

## [22:20] The honest limits

Now let me be fair about what this story is not.
Aravind is a hospital, run by a charitable trust. Your firm is not. Cataract surgery is one operation, repeated hundreds of thousands of times a year. Two tables per surgeon only make sense when the queue never ends. Some of Aravind's early vision centres were funded by grants. And a 40-person firm cannot run a two-year training school.
Two more cautions. Many of the figures in this story come from Aravind itself: its reports, its papers, its leaders speaking to journalists. They are careful figures, but they are its own. And the comparisons with Britain and America use different measures and different years, so I have kept them broad on purpose.
So I am not asking you to copy Aravind. I am asking you to copy one question.

## [23:15] Act 4: What this means for a business of 15 to 100 people

Here are four lessons I take from Aravind for a business of 15 to 100 people. Each one comes from a moment in the story. None of them needs software. Each of them needs an afternoon, a pen, and the honesty to look at your own week.

## [23:35] Lesson one: list every step, and ask which ones need you

Remember the surgeon on her stool, turning from one table to the other. Six minutes of surgery. Everything else done by someone else.
Do the same with your most important process. Write down every step. Every one. For a quote, it might be: enquiry received, enquiry logged, drawing checked, cost worked out, price decided, quote typed, quote sent, follow-up call, revision, order confirmed.
Now go down the list with a pen. Next to each step, write "needs me" or "does not need me". Be strict. Most owners find that only the price and perhaps one call truly need them. The other eight steps are waiting on the owner only because nobody else was ever given them.
That list is the start of the design. [your own line]
One caution. Do not try to do this for the whole business at once. Aravind began with one operation, done thousands of times. Start with one process, the one that lands on your desk most often. Get that one right. Then move to the next.

## [24:50] Lesson two: give every other step a trained person and a written standard

Remember the young women who make up nearly two-thirds of Aravind's staff, and the two years Aravind spends training them.
You do not need two years. But every step that does not need you needs two things. A named person. And a written standard for how it is done.
Take dispatch. Who checks the packing against the order? Who books the transport? Who sends the client the docket number? Who confirms delivery? If the answer to each is "it depends", the answer is really "the owner, in the end". Give each one a name. Write the standard on one page. Then that step has a home.
The standard does not need to be long. Aravind's counselling checklist fits on a page. Yours can be five lines: what is checked, by whom, by when, where it is recorded, and who is told when it is done. If the person who owns the step is on leave, someone else can pick up the page and do it the same way.

## [26:00] Lesson three: a standard is not a cage

Remember the counselling checklist. A first-year staff member, often eighteen or nineteen years old, explaining aftercare to a patient as well as a senior would.
Many owners worry that writing things down will make their people rigid. Or that their experienced staff will feel insulted. My experience is the opposite. A standard is not a cage. It is what lets a new person be good in week one. And it frees the experienced person from answering the same question forty times.
Think of a client file in a professional firm. What documents must be in it? What must be checked before it goes to the partner? Write that down once. Your newest assistant can then open a file and know exactly what good looks like.
And remember the trainees in the Aravind study. Their mistakes were counted, and the count led to a better way to learn. A written standard does the same for you. When something goes wrong, you can see which step slipped, and fix the step instead of blaming the person.

## [27:10] Lesson four: follow-up is a step with a home, not a favour

Remember the visit at one month. Every patient. Planned before they leave the hospital.
In most firms, follow-up is a favour. Somebody remembers to call about the quote. Somebody remembers to chase the payment. When they are busy, they forget, and the owner finds out last.
At Aravind, follow-up is a step with a day, a place and a person. You can do the same. Every quote sent gets a follow-up date the day it is sent. Every invoice gets a reminder date. Every client meeting gets a next step written before anyone leaves the room. Then the follow-up shows up on a list, and anyone can see whether it happened.
Then, once a week, look at the list. What was due? What was done? What is late? That is your Friday score. You stop being the follow-up department, because the follow-up has a department of its own: a date, a name and a list.
Four lessons. List the steps. Give each one a person and a standard. Treat the standard as a help, not a cage. And give follow-up a home.

## [28:25] Close

In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, I did this exercise first on our own work. I listed the steps of our most important process and asked which ones truly needed the people at the top. Then I gave every other step a name, a date and a next step, on one sheet that everyone can see. We run on it every day. [your own line]
What surprised me was not the sheet. It was how few steps truly needed the senior people, once we wrote them all down. And how much calmer the week became when the follow-ups had a home of their own.
This is the work I do now, at Venture Drafters. I sit with an owner, we take one process, and we design it so the owner's hour goes on the work only the owner can do.
Aravind is not a story about working harder. Its surgeons do not work harder than yours. Its system simply asks less of them that is not theirs to do.
Dr V started with eleven beds and one question. You can start with one process and the same question.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.

Thank you for watching. I will see you next week.

script:
## [0:00] February 2009

February 2009. A neighbourhood grocery shop in an Indian city. The shutter is down in the middle of the day. For weeks, the shelves have been thinning. The suppliers stopped sending stock when their bills stopped being paid. The staff have not had a salary since October.
This shop is one of about sixteen hundred. They belong to a chain called Subhiksha. By the end of the month, every one of them has stopped trading.
The same month, in Mumbai, another supermarket opens at the usual hour. It belongs to a chain that has been trading for seven years and has not yet reached twenty-five stores. The chain is called DMart.
The two chains sold the same things. Everyday groceries. Prices below the printed MRP. A short list of items. Suppliers paid quickly, in return for a discount. On paper, they were cousins.

## [1:05] The question

One of them had sixteen hundred stores, and lost them all. The other took twenty-four years to reach five hundred, and it is still growing.
What made the difference? Not the idea. Not the founder's intelligence. Both men were very able. The difference was a few numbers, watched on a fixed rhythm, and the discipline to let those numbers set the pace.
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [1:30] Act 1. Your desk first

I want to start with your desk, not theirs.
Picture a trading firm in Indore. Forty people. Fifteen crore in sales. Two godowns. It has had a good year. The bank has offered a bigger limit. A large customer wants you to open a depot in Dewas. A relative says a second branch is the obvious next step. Everyone around you is saying the same word. Expand.
Now ask yourself three quiet questions. How many days of stock are sitting in your godowns today? How many days do you take, on average, to pay your suppliers? And how many days do your customers take to pay you?
If you can answer those from one screen, in one minute, you are ready to talk about Dewas. If the answers live in your head, or in your accountant's head, or in a register that is updated at the month end, then the second branch is not a plan. It is a bet.
Most owners I meet can answer the first question roughly, the second question never, and the third question only by phoning someone. They are not careless. They are busy. They are the memory of the business, and the memory is full.
Both men in today's story faced the same choice you face. Grow, and how fast. They answered it very differently.

## [2:45] Subhiksha, Chennai, 1997

The first man is R. Subramanian. He studied at IIT Madras and IIM Ahmedabad, and ran a financial services business in Chennai. In March 1997 he opened a small grocery shop in Thiruvanmiyur, in south Chennai. He called it Subhiksha.
The design was careful. The shops were small and plain. No air-conditioning. No fancy lighting. They sat just off the main road, where the rent is lower. Customers lived within about two kilometres and came on foot or on a two-wheeler. The range was capped at about fifteen hundred items, only the fastest movers. Goods were bought for cash, directly from manufacturers, to earn the biggest discount. And prices were about eight per cent below MRP. That is how Business Today described the chain in 2004.
It worked. By 2002 and 2003 there were about a hundred and forty stores, across thirty towns in Tamil Nadu. ICICI Venture had taken a ten per cent stake. This was a serious, well-run business with a clear idea.

## [3:50] DMart, Powai, 2002

The second man is Radhakishan Damani. By the late 1990s he was one of the better-known value investors in the Indian stock market. That is how his own company describes him. In 2000 he conceived DMart. In 2002 he opened the first store, in Powai, in Mumbai.
His idea came from the same family. The company calls it everyday low cost, everyday low price. Do not run a sale on Sunday and recover it on Monday. Keep costs so low that the price can stay low every day. Carry a narrower range than the rivals. Buy directly from manufacturers. Pay suppliers on time, and take the discount for paying promptly.
One more choice set DMart apart. It preferred to own the building, or to take land on a lease of more than thirty years and build on it. That made every store expensive to open. It also meant no landlord could raise the rent, or ask it to leave.
The first store outside Maharashtra opened in Gujarat in 2007. By the year ending March 2010, eight years after the first store, the count had just crossed twenty-five.

## [5:00] A promise is not a system

So here are two founders. Both clever. Both careful about cost. Both with the same promise to the customer. Everyday goods, at a low price, every day.
But a promise is not a system. A promise is something you say. A system is something that tells you, every week, whether you are keeping it.
Think about the chain of things that promise depends on. Low prices need low costs. Low costs need stock that moves fast, because stock that sits costs you rent, interest and spoilage. Paying suppliers early needs cash. Cash needs stock that turns into sales before the next bill falls due.
Every one of those links can be counted. So the question for the rest of this episode is simple. In each company, who was counting, how often, and what did they do when the count said slow down?

## [6:00] Act 2. Five plain mechanisms

Let us open DMart's machine. Most of what follows comes from one document. It is the offer document the company filed with SEBI in 2017, before it listed on the stock exchanges. It is unusually plain about how the stores run.
I found five mechanisms. None of them is clever. Each one could be explained to a new store manager in five minutes. That is the point. A system that needs a genius to run it is not a system. Here they are, one at a time.

## [6:35] Mechanism one: a short list

The first mechanism is a short list.
DMart carries a narrower range than most large stores. The offer document says the company keeps a strong focus on what it calls product assortment, so that stock does not build up. Business Today reported in 2018 that Damani prefers fewer brands, because too many brands confuse the customer and fill the back room with stock.
I want to be honest with you here. You will see a precise figure on social media for how many items DMart stocks. I could not trace that figure to the company, or to any reliable report. So I will not give you one. What the record supports is the direction. Fewer items than the rivals, chosen with care.
And remember, Subhiksha also kept a short list. About fifteen hundred items. So a short list, on its own, does not save anyone.
What a short list does is make counting possible. If you carry fifteen thousand items, nobody can watch each one. If you carry a few thousand, chosen because they sell, you can give every one of them a number and a rule.
That brings us to the second mechanism.

## [8:05] Mechanism two: every item has a number

The second mechanism is that every item, in every store, has a written number that decides when to re-order it.
Here is how the offer document describes it. Every item has a bar code. When it is scanned at the till, the sale is recorded. The stock of every item, in every store, is tracked every day. That information reaches the distribution centres and the head office daily.
Then comes the important part. Each store has its own re-order level for each item. It is set from three things. How much the shelf is meant to display. How long the supplier takes to deliver. And how many units the item sells on an average day. When stock falls to that level, it is time to order. The company says these levels are reviewed continuously, to catch changes in season and trend.
Think about what that means. This is the first question of our series. Where does the work live?
At DMart, the decision to re-order does not live in a store manager's memory. It does not live in a phone call from the supplier's salesman. It lives in a number, written against every item, in every store. The store manager can be new. The salesman can be persuasive. The number does not change because someone is new or persuasive. It changes when the sales change.
The document adds two more plain rules. Orders are placed from the data, and the company calls its buying conservative, to keep expired goods off the shelf. And stock moves first in, first out. Old stock is sold before new stock.
Now look at your own business. A distributor of pipes. A wholesaler of rice. A pharma stockist. When does a re-order happen? Usually when someone notices the rack is empty, or when the supplier's man calls. That is re-ordering by memory. DMart re-orders by a written level.

## [10:15] Mechanism three: pay in a week

The third mechanism is the one I find most interesting. It is not on the shelf. It is in the supplier ledger.
DMart pays its suppliers fast. The company publishes a number called days payable. It is the average number of days it takes to pay for what it buys. In the year to March 2020, it was about eight days. In the pandemic year, it rose to about nine. Since then it has stayed between six and a little over seven. In the year to March 2026, it was 7.2 days. Business Today reported in 2018 that DMart paid within ten days, when other chains took about a month. So, on the record, roughly a week to ten days.
Why pay so fast? The offer document says it plainly. The company pays its suppliers on time, and is often able to get a discount for paying promptly. That discount is part of how the price stays low.
Now put this next to the stock. DMart holds about thirty days of stock. It pays for that stock in about seven. So at any moment, about three weeks of the stock on its shelves has been paid for with DMart's own money. Not the supplier's. Not the bank's. That is my reading of its published numbers, and the arithmetic is simple.
That is the feedback loop. This is question three of our series. Who finds out when something slips, and how fast? At DMart, if an item stops selling, there is no supplier credit to hide behind. The cash tied up in that item shows up within weeks. The money itself raises its hand.
Compare that with a common habit in Indian trade. Buy on sixty or ninety days of credit. Hold the stock as long as you like. The supplier is funding your slow stock, so nobody notices that it is slow. You find out last. Usually at the year end, when the stock-taking shows dead stock that nobody remembers ordering.
DMart chose the opposite. It chose to feel slow stock immediately. And its suppliers pay it a discount for the privilege.

## [12:45] Mechanism four: the same few numbers, every year

The fourth mechanism is a handful of numbers, measured the same way every year.
Open any of DMart's investor presentations. You will find the same short set of charts. Number of stores. Retail area. Sales per square foot. Growth in stores that are at least two years old. Days of inventory. Days payable. Inventory turnover. Return on capital. Under each chart is a one-line definition of how it is calculated. The definitions do not move.
Here is the inventory turnover. That is sales divided by average stock. In the year to March 2014, 14.3. In 2015, 14.0. In 2016, 14.2. In 2020, 14.2 again. In 2023, 14.8. In 2024, 14.6. Year after year, around fourteen. In plain words, the whole stock is sold and bought again about fourteen times a year.
And the days of inventory. 30.4 in 2020. 36.5 in the pandemic year. Then 33.3, then 28.8, then 29.2. Business Today reported in 2018 that rival chains held sixty to seventy days. That rival figure is one magazine's estimate, so treat it as a rough comparison, not a fact.
This answers question two. How can anyone see the state of the work? At DMart, the state of the whole company is a few numbers, on one page, defined once.
Now, a careful point. Those charts are what DMart shows investors, once a quarter and once a year. Inside the company, the data is daily. What its managers actually look at every week is not public. I do not know what is on a DMart manager's desk on a Friday, and I will not pretend to.
But the pattern is clear. A few numbers. The same definitions. Watched often enough that a slip in one of them is seen while it is still small. That is the Friday score, in a listed company's clothes.

## [15:00] Mechanism five: the next store near the last one

The fifth mechanism is about growth itself. DMart has a rule for where the next store goes.
It is called a cluster. New stores open within a few kilometres of existing stores and distribution centres. The company deepens a region before it enters a new one. The offer document says this gives it a better understanding of local needs, and a cheaper, steadier supply chain.
Add the ownership choice. Owning the building is expensive, and DMart says so itself. In its offer document, the company warned investors that the ownership model needs more capital for each store, so it may not be able to expand at its historical rate. It is rare to see a company write its own speed limit into a prospectus.
Look at the pace. From 2002, it took about eight years to cross twenty-five stores. In the year to March 2012 it opened ten stores. Then seven. Then thirteen. Then fourteen. Then twenty-one. Twenty-one was the most it had ever opened in a year. By March 2017, the month it listed, it had a hundred and thirty-one stores.
Since then it has picked up speed, carefully. 214 stores in 2020. 284 in 2022. 365 in 2024. 415 in 2025. And 500 in March 2026.
Here is the comparison that sums up this episode. Subhiksha added roughly fifteen hundred stores in about two years. DMart took about twenty-four years to reach five hundred.
Slow is not a weakness here. It is a design choice. Each new store sits close to a distribution centre that already knows how to feed it. Each one opens only when the company can pay for the building. The growth sits on top of the counting. Never in front of it.

## [17:05] When the founder is not in the room

Two more questions from our series. How are errors caught? And what happens when the owner is away?
Errors first. The offer document lists plain controls. First in, first out. Conservative buying to avoid expiry. Checks against stock shortage and theft. Bags screened at the exit. CCTV in the stores. None of this is clever. All of it is routine. And routine is what catches errors before they reach the customer.
Now the owner. Damani is famously private. He has not been the operating head. A professional managing director, Navil Noronha, ran them for many years. In January 2026 Noronha stepped down at the end of his term. Anshul Asawa took over as chief executive on the first of February, and became managing director in April.
In the quarter of that handover, the company opened fifty-eight stores. A record. It crossed five hundred. One quarter is not a verdict. But the numbers did not wait for the founder, or for the long-serving chief. The work still went out on Monday.

## [18:00] Act 3. Every system is tested

Every system is tested. Sometimes by a crisis. Sometimes by a bad year. Most often, by its own success, when growth arrives faster than the counting.
Subhiksha's test was the scale-up. DMart's tests were a pandemic and, now, the ten-minute delivery app. Let us take them in that order.

## [18:20] Subhiksha: fifteen hundred stores in two years

In September 2006, Subhiksha had about a hundred and sixty stores, nearly all in Tamil Nadu. That July it had announced a national rollout. Delhi, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka. The plan was more than six hundred stores by the end of 2007.
It went much further. Six hundred and seventy stores by March 2007. Thirteen hundred and twenty by March 2008. About sixteen hundred and fifty by September 2008. Business Today counted roughly fifteen hundred stores added in twenty-four months. The chain also added mobile phones and medicines.
How was this paid for? Mostly by borrowing. Between late 2004 and early 2007, Business Today reports, the company raised about a hundred and sixty crore of equity, two hundred and twenty crore of debt, and a bridge loan of a hundred and twenty-five crore. In March 2008, Azim Premji's investment arm bought a ten per cent stake from ICICI Venture, for about two hundred and thirty crore. Reported sales had nearly tripled in a year, to about twenty-three hundred crore.
From the outside, it looked like a triumph. That year, the Boston Consulting Group named it among fifty fast-rising companies from emerging markets.

## [19:20] October 2008: the cycle stops

Then the cycle broke.
Subhiksha had planned to raise fresh equity in 2008. In September, global markets fell. The equity did not come. The bridge loan was due. The banks would not lend more without new equity. The founder later told Knowledge at Wharton that the company ran out of cash by October 2008, although, he said, it had been profitable until September.
Now remember how the model worked. Subhiksha bought for cash. That was how it earned its discounts. So when the cash stopped, the buying stopped. No cash, no fresh stock. No fresh stock, empty shelves. Empty shelves, fewer customers. Fewer customers, less cash.
By January 2009, about fifteen thousand employees had not been paid since October. Salary dues were about twenty crore. Money owed to suppliers was about forty-five crore. Unpaid security guards stopped coming. In February, reports said about six hundred stores and warehouses had been ransacked or looted. By the end of that month, operations had stopped.

## [20:20] What the record says, and what it does not

Why did it happen? I will tell you only what is on the record.
The founder blamed cash flow, not the discount model. He said the company was over-confident about raising equity, and should have raised it in March 2008. Business Today's account adds that working capital was used to open new stores, and that new states were opened together, not one after another. Arvind Singhal of Technopak said the model was sound, but the money went into stores rather than into the supply chain, logistics and people.
Those are explanations. They are not court findings. Investors asked for an independent audit. The Madras High Court later ordered the company wound up, on a bank's petition. In 2018 the Enforcement Directorate arrested the founder, alleging that bank loans had been diverted. I found no final judgment in that case. Those remain allegations. A separate case, over deposits taken by another company, has its own court record. It is outside this story.
So I will not draw a lesson about anyone's character. I will draw one about design.

## [21:00] The companion: Target Canada

This pattern is not only Indian. In 2013, Target, the large American discount chain, opened stores across Canada. It planned a hundred and twenty-four stores in one year.
To stock them, staff had to enter data for about seventy-five thousand products into a new computer system, on a rigid schedule. An internal check later estimated that the item data was right only about thirty per cent of the time. In Target's American business, the figure was ninety-eight to ninety-nine per cent. Wrong sizes, wrong case quantities, wrong delivery details.
The result was the strangest sight in retail. Empty shelves in the stores, and overflowing warehouses at the same time. About two years after opening, Target Canada sought protection from its creditors. About seventeen thousand six hundred people lost their jobs.
A different country, and different details. The same shape. The stores grew faster than the system that counts what is in them.

## [22:00] DMart's tests: a pandemic and the ten-minute app

DMart's tests are on the record too. In the pandemic year, to March 2021, revenue fell, from about twenty-four thousand seven hundred crore to about twenty-three thousand eight hundred crore. Sales in older stores fell thirteen per cent. Days of stock rose from about thirty to thirty-six and a half. Within two years, they were back under twenty-nine.
The live test is quick commerce. In October 2024, the managing director said, and I quote, "We clearly see impact of online grocery formats." Growth in older stores slowed from about ten per cent to about eight. DMart cut its own delivery service from twenty-five cities to eighteen. In the year it opened a record eighty-five stores, and its lease liabilities nearly doubled. Its own numbers moved. Days of stock rose from 29.2 to 33.2 in two years. Return on capital eased from about nineteen per cent to about seventeen. Revenue still grew about sixteen per cent last year.
The test is not finished. But notice how we know any of this. The same few numbers, printed the same way. That is a system telling the truth about itself.

## [23:00] Act 4. What this means for a firm of 15 to 100 people

Let me bring this back to your business. You do not run five hundred supermarkets. You may run a factory in Pithampur, a distribution business in Indore, or a CA firm with twenty-five people. The scale is different. The arithmetic is the same.
Here are four lessons I take from these two companies.

## [23:25] Lesson one: growth is limited by the system that counts what you have

Lesson one. Growth is limited by the system that counts what you have.
Subhiksha could open stores at a remarkable pace. In the end, it could not fund and fill them. Target Canada could open over a hundred stores in a year. Its system did not know what was inside them. DMart opened ten stores in a year, then seven, then thirteen, because every new store had to be counted, supplied and paid for by a system that already worked.
In your business, the new store is a new branch, a new salesman, a new product line, or ten new clients. Before you add one, ask a plain question. Can I count what I already have, today, without phoning anyone?
For a distributor, that means stock by item, by godown. For a manufacturer, it means every open order and its promised date. For a professional firm, it means every open client file, with a name, a due date and a next step.
If the count lives in people's heads, adding more will not grow the business. It will grow the confusion. And you will be the last to find out.

## [24:40] Lesson two: a few numbers on a weekly rhythm

Lesson two. A few numbers on a weekly rhythm beat a hundred numbers once a quarter.
DMart shows the world about eight numbers, defined the same way for years. Inside, its data is daily. Most owners I meet have the opposite. A thick report from the accountant, once a quarter, with a hundred lines, read once and filed.
A hundred numbers once a quarter tell you what went wrong three months ago. Four numbers every Friday tell you what is going wrong this week, while it is still small.
What would your four be? For a trader, I would suggest days of stock, days you take to pay suppliers, days your customers take to pay you, and orders that went out late this week. For a manufacturer, orders due this week, orders late, rejections, and raw material below its re-order level. For a CA firm, files due this week, files overdue, files waiting on the client, and files waiting on a partner.
Put them on one screen. Look at them every Friday. Hand out the work on Monday. That is the whole rhythm. It is not glamorous. Neither is DMart's.
[your own line]

## [25:55] Lesson three: cash discount discipline is a system, not a negotiation

Lesson three. Cash discount discipline is a system, not a negotiation.
Most owners treat a supplier's cash discount as something to bargain for, month by month. Say two per cent, if you pay within seven days. Some months you take it. Some months the money is stuck in stock or with a customer, so you do not. When a supplier calls asking "ho gaya?", the honest answer is, it depends on the month.
At DMart, paying in about a week is not a decision someone makes each month. It is the result of stock that turns about fourteen times a year. The fast payment is an output of the system. The discount is the reward.
Subhiksha shows the other side. It also bought for cash, to earn discounts. But its cash was going into new stores. When the cash stopped, the buying stopped, and the shelves emptied within weeks.
So in your business, the discipline starts on the day the purchase bill arrives. A pay-by date, written against it, that same day. Stock days known, so you know whether the cash will be there. And a Friday look at everything that falls due next week. Do that, and the discount stops being a negotiation. It becomes a habit the business can afford.

## [27:05] Lesson four: slow and steady is a design choice

Lesson four. Slow and steady is a design choice.
DMart wrote its own speed limit into its offer document. It said that owning its stores could slow its growth, and it chose to own them anyway. That was not timidity. It was a rule, written down before the opportunity arrived.
You can do the same. Write your rule before the large order or the new branch walks in. For example, we open the next branch only when the first one has run for six months with its stock and payment numbers inside our limits. The numbers are yours to choose. The point is to choose them when you are calm, not when the opportunity is standing in your office.
In the end, what the owner looks at every Friday decides what the business becomes. Subhiksha's plans, as announced, were written in store counts. DMart's reports are written in stock days and cash. Each became what it watched.

## [28:00] Close

In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, we did not start with a big system. We started with one process. Every piece of work got a name, a date and a next step, on one sheet that anyone could see. On Friday, we look at the same few numbers. On Monday, the work goes out.
This is the work I do now, for owners of businesses with fifteen to a hundred people. I set up the system on your own sheet, train your team on it, and keep it running with you.
