script:
## [00:00] Cold open: the stand at dawn

It is early morning at a busy Indian airport. An Airbus A320, in blue and white, rolls onto a remote stand and stops on its mark.
Before the engines have fully wound down, the ground crew moves. Chocks go under the wheels. A ramp is pushed to the front door. Another goes to the rear. A belt loader backs up to the hold.
Nobody is shouting. Nobody is on the phone to the owner. Each person on that apron knows their part, and the order in which it happens.
Passengers walk down. Cleaners walk up. Bags come out, and other bags go in. In about half an hour, the same aircraft will push back, full again.
On this airline, a scene like this repeats more than two thousand times a day.

## [00:50] The question

IndiGo flew its first flight in August 2006. It entered an industry where most airlines were losing money. Within six years, it was the largest airline in India.
It did not get there with the best food or the widest seats. It got there with one promise that any passenger can check on a wristwatch. The plane leaves when it says it will.
So here is the question for this episode. How do you keep one promise thousands of times a day, when the founder is not standing on the apron?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [01:30] An industry that ate airlines

Let me set the scene as it was in 2005.
Indian aviation was full of new airlines, cheap tickets and large plans. Many of them would not last. Kingfisher stopped flying in 2012. Jet Airways, for years the biggest private airline, stopped in 2019. Go First stopped in 2023.
Airlines are a hard business for an owner. The aircraft is expensive. Fuel is priced in dollars. The fare is set by the cheapest rival on the route. And every delay costs money in ways that are hard to see. A late aircraft means crew paid for hours they did not fly. It means passengers who miss connections. It means the next flight, and the one after that, leaving late too.
If you run a business, you know this kind of arithmetic. A margin that looks healthy on paper, and then quietly disappears into the small costs of things going wrong.

## [02:35] One hundred aircraft before the first flight

Into this industry came two founders. Rahul Bhatia ran InterGlobe, a travel business in Delhi. Rakesh Gangwal was an airline executive based in the United States.
In June 2005, before a single passenger had flown, they placed a firm order with Airbus for one hundred aircraft. All of them the same model, the A320. The value at list prices was reported at around six billion dollars.
Airbus itself did not take the order seriously at first. Its own executives later admitted as much, in Tarun Shukla's book on the airline, Sky High.
The first aircraft arrived in July 2006. The first flight left on the fourth of August.
An order for one hundred aircraft sounds like ambition. I read it as something else. It was a design decision, made before the first customer. It said: we will grow, and every aircraft we add will be the same as the last one.

## [03:35] How a delay travels

Think about how a delay travels through an airline.
One aircraft flies several flights in a day. If the first flight of the morning leaves twenty minutes late, the second starts late too. The crew's duty hours run out sooner. The next airport has to hold a gate. By evening, one small delay in the morning can be an hour.
The same thing happens on a shop floor. The raw material arrives late, so the job starts late, so the dispatch is late, so the customer calls. And whom does the customer call? Not the person who was late. The customer calls the owner.
In most businesses, the owner is the one who notices the chain. The owner is the memory, the follow-up department and the feedback loop. Every slip ends up on one desk.
An airline cannot work like that. There are too many flights and too many people. Nobody can stand at every gate. So IndiGo had to answer the same question you face. How do you design the work so that it keeps its promise without someone chasing it?

## [04:50] Choosing the promise

Most businesses make several promises at once. Best quality. Lowest price. Fastest service. Personal attention. Each one pulls the work in a different direction.
IndiGo picked one promise that a customer could check without asking anyone. Was the plane on time, or not? The departure time is printed on the ticket. The customer has a watch. There is nothing to argue about.
Notice that this is a promise about the work, not about the brand. You cannot keep it with advertising. You can only keep it with the way the work is organised, every day, by people the founders will never meet.
Its first television film, a few years after launch, was built on that one idea. The line the agency remembers is "On time is such a wonderful thing."
That promise became the test for every other decision. If something helped the plane leave on time, it stayed. If something made it harder, it went. Let us look at what that meant in practice. I count five parts to the system.

## [06:00] Part one: one aircraft type

The first part is the simplest to say and the hardest to keep. One aircraft type.
For more than ten years, IndiGo flew one aircraft family, the Airbus A320. Same cockpit. Same manuals.
Think about what that does.
Training. A pilot trained on one aircraft can fly any aircraft in the fleet. So can the cabin crew. When someone calls in sick, the replacement does not need a different licence.
Spares. One store of parts covers every aircraft. You do not keep a shelf of parts for a type you fly twice a week.
Maintenance. Engineers see the same faults again and again, so they learn them. The checks are the same. The tools are the same.
Scheduling. Any aircraft can take any route. If one aircraft has a fault in Kolkata, another can take its place without a change of crew or catering.
When the airline listed on the stock exchange in 2015, its offer document showed what this was worth. Its cost to fly one seat for one kilometre was about six US cents. SpiceJet's was a little under seven. Jet Airways' was about nine. Leave fuel out, and IndiGo's cost was the lowest of any Indian airline. Analysts linked that largely to the single aircraft type and a young fleet.
Now, an honest note. IndiGo did not keep one type forever. In 2017 it added small ATR turboprops for regional routes. It said it would run them as a separate unit, to keep the main operation free of the complexity of a second type. Today it also flies larger A321s, and it has ordered wide-body aircraft for long routes.
But look at the order of events. It held to one type for more than ten years, while it learnt to run the system. It added a second type only when the network needed it. And it put a fence around it when it did.
For an owner, the translation is plain. How many versions of the same job does your firm run? Three formats of quotation. Four ways to raise an invoice. A different dispatch routine for each salesman's customers. Every version is a second aircraft type. Somebody has to remember how each one works. Usually, that somebody is you.

## [08:25] Part two: the turn

The second part is the turn. The time an aircraft spends on the ground between landing and taking off again.
An aircraft on the ground earns nothing. So a low-cost airline wants that time as short as it can safely make it. In 2012, Business Today reported that IndiGo was aiming for a twenty-minute turn. In 2022, an IndiGo executive put the usual turn at thirty to thirty-five minutes. Treat the first as an aim and the second as the working figure.
What happens in that half hour? The sequence is common across the industry. The aircraft stops on its mark. Chocks go in. Doors open. Passengers come off. Bags come out of the hold. Cleaners go through the cabin. Fuel and catering go in where needed. New bags are loaded. New passengers board. Doors close. Papers are signed. The aircraft pushes back.
The point is not the list. The point is that many of these steps happen at the same time, and each one has an owner. The person on the belt loader does not wait for the cleaners. The fuel crew does not wait to be told. Each lane runs on its own clock, and the clocks meet at the door closing.
IndiGo added small details to save minutes. Business Standard reports that it has used ramps rather than steep step-ladders from its first day. A ramp is quicker for most passengers and easier for those who need help. In 2022 it began letting passengers off through three doors instead of two. The airline said its trials cut the time to empty an aircraft from about thirteen minutes to about seven or eight. One outside commentator doubted the full gain. Even so, the company estimated three to five minutes saved per turn at remote stands. Across thousands of turns a day, minutes like these decide whether an aircraft flies one more trip or not.
Here is the part I want an owner to notice. A good turn is not run by a station manager shouting. It is run by a sequence everyone has learnt, and by ground staff who work to a written checklist. The state of the turn is visible to anyone on the apron. The bags are still coming out, or they are not. The ramp is at the door, or it is not.
That is what I mean when I say work needs a home. On the apron, every step has a name, a time and a next step. No owner has to walk across and ask, "ho gaya?"

## [11:15] Part three: one number everyone can see

The third part is a number. The share of flights that leave on time.
Here aviation has something most businesses do not. The aviation regulator publishes on-time performance every month, airline by airline, at the country's largest airports. Nobody can hide from it. The passenger can read it. The rival can read it. The ground staff can read it.
IndiGo made this number its public face. In 2010 it said about nine in ten of its flights over the previous four months had been on time. In the regulator's monthly reports it was at or near the top in most months. In March 2025, for example, it recorded about eighty-eight per cent at the four largest airports, ahead of Akasa at about eighty-seven and the Air India group at about eighty-two. In August 2025, when the table covered six airports, it was above ninety per cent.
Inside any airline, a number like this is only useful if it comes with reasons. Late because the aircraft came in late. Late because of weather. Late because a passenger did not turn up at the gate. Late because of a technical fault. Airlines everywhere record each delay against a standard reason code for exactly this purpose. The number tells you how you did. The reasons tell you what to fix.
I want to be fair here. In 2012, rival airlines told Business Standard, off the record, that IndiGo kept its record partly by printing longer flight times on its schedule. If the timetable allows more time, you are more likely to arrive on time. IndiGo did not answer that charge then, and some padding is common across airlines. But it is a reminder that any score can be bent, and that an owner should read the reasons as well as the score.
For a business of forty people, this is the Friday score. One number for the promise you made. Quotes sent on time. Orders delivered as committed. And beside it, every week, the short list of why the misses happened.

## [13:30] Part four: saying no

The fourth part is the one owners find hardest. Saying no.
For its first eighteen years, IndiGo flew one cabin. No business class. Food was sold on board, not handed out free. When it listed in 2015, it did not sell connecting tickets with other airlines, so another airline's delay could not become its delay.
Each of those is a decision not to add a step to the turn. A business cabin needs different catering, different boarding and different seats to clean. A free meal must be loaded on every flight. A connecting ticket means waiting for someone else's aircraft.
Aditya Ghosh, who led the airline as its president for about a decade, once described the approach at a management conference. In my words, not his: the airline chose to do without a grand vision statement, and to be steady and predictable instead.
The money side followed the same logic. IndiGo bought aircraft from Airbus on large-order terms, sold them to leasing companies, and leased them back. It is called sale and leaseback. In 2017, 118 of its 131 aircraft were on lease. The method kept the fleet young, because leased aircraft go back after a fixed term and new ones arrive. Younger aircraft break down less. Critics argued that part of the airline's profit came from these deals rather than from flying. IndiGo said it spread any gains across the life of each lease. Both views are on the record.
And yes, it later said yes to some things. In late 2024 it launched a business product on busy routes, and a loyalty programme. But it said no for eighteen years first, while the core promise was set.
For an owner, saying no sounds like this. No to the one customer who wants a special packing format. No to a custom report for one client every month. No to a fourth product line before the third one runs cleanly. Complexity is not a cost you pay once. You pay it every day, at every handover.

## [15:45] Part five: the founders are not on the apron

Now the question I ask in every episode. What happens when the owner is away?
At IndiGo, the owners were away from the start. Rakesh Gangwal lived in the United States. Rahul Bhatia ran a group of businesses. Neither of them was on the ramp at six in the morning. Professional managers ran the airline day to day.
So the work had to live somewhere other than in the founders' heads. It lived in the fleet plan, the schedule, the turn sequence, the crew roster and the monthly number.
And it grew. In July 2012 IndiGo became the largest domestic airline, with about twenty-seven per cent of passengers. By 2015 it was near thirty-seven per cent. By 2023 it carried more than sixty per cent of India's domestic passengers. By late 2025 it was running more than 2,700 flights a day.
No founder can follow up on 2,700 flights a day. Only a design can.

## [16:45] The other design

It helps to see the road not taken. In this case, it was taken in the same year.
Kingfisher Airlines began flying in May 2005, with four new A320s between Mumbai and Delhi. Its design was the opposite of IndiGo's. It offered a full-service experience, with meals and a screen at every seat. In 2007 it took over the low-cost airline Air Deccan. It flew ATR turboprops, A320 family jets, and from 2008, wide-body A330s to London. More aircraft types. More cabins. More kinds of customer.
Until late 2011, it was the second-largest domestic airline. It was reported never to have made a profit. In 2012, its staff went unpaid for months. In October 2012, the regulator suspended its licence. It did not fly again.
I want to be careful here. Many things went into that outcome: debt, fuel prices, taxes and decisions taken at the top. People lost their jobs and their wages, and that deserves respect. I am not saying one choice caused it. I am saying the two airlines show two designs. One kept adding. The other kept saying no. In 2012, the year Kingfisher stopped flying, IndiGo became the largest airline in India.

## [18:00] Every system meets a bad year

Every system looks good in a calm year. The real question is what happens in a bad one.
IndiGo has had several. They are worth looking at honestly, because in some of them the design bent and held, and in one of them it did not.

## [18:20] The engines

The first test came from a supplier. Many of IndiGo's newer aircraft use engines made by Pratt and Whitney. In 2023, a manufacturing problem was found in some engine parts, and engines around the world had to come off early for inspection.
For IndiGo, that meant aircraft standing on the ground with nothing wrong with the aircraft itself. In November 2023 it said about forty-five were already grounded, with more to come. At the peak, in the middle of 2024, about seventy-five stood idle. By May 2025, that was down to the forties.
Here, the design bent. The airline leased extra aircraft with crews from other operators. It kept older aircraft flying for longer. Notice the irony. To keep its promise, the one-type airline had to fly other people's aircraft, including Boeing jets. The rule bent so that the promise did not break.

## [19:20] The pandemic, and the day the computers stopped

The second test was the pandemic. In the year to March 2021, IndiGo lost about 5,806 crore rupees. The next year, it lost about 6,162 crore. Every airline in the world was hurt. But by the year to March 2024, IndiGo reported a record profit of about 8,172 crore. A simple, standard operation is easier to shrink, and easier to start again.
The third test was smaller, and it tells you something about the people. On the nineteenth of July 2024, a faulty software update crashed computers running Windows around the world. Airline check-in systems went down. At several Indian airports, IndiGo staff wrote boarding passes by hand, and passengers posted photographs of them. It was slow. There were cancellations. But the staff knew the sequence well enough to run part of it on paper.

## [20:15] December 2025: the week it did not bend

The fourth test is the one that matters most for this story, because the system did not hold.
The regulator had issued new rules on pilot rest. They limited night landings and night duties, to reduce fatigue. The second phase came into force on the first of November 2025. Airlines had known the rules were coming for more than a year.
In November, IndiGo cancelled 1,232 flights. It told the regulator that 755 of those were because of crew and duty-time limits. Then, in the first week of December, the network gave way. On the third of December, fewer than one in five of its flights left on time. On the fourth, fewer than one in ten. Between the third and the fifth, it cancelled 2,507 flights and delayed 1,852 more. More than three lakh passengers were caught in those three days alone.
The regulator gave the airline temporary relief from some of the new rules, ordered it to cut its schedule, and set up an inquiry. The findings came out in January 2026. In plain words, the inquiry found that the airline had been run to use every pilot, every aircraft and every route as fully as possible, leaving almost no margin to absorb a shock. It also pointed to weak preparation for the new rules, gaps in management control, and the software used to plan crew.
The regulator fined the airline about twenty-two crore rupees. It warned the chief executive and other senior managers. It required a bank guarantee of fifty crore, tied to reforms. The airline's board accepted the findings. In March 2026, the chief executive stepped down, citing personal reasons, and Rahul Bhatia took interim charge. The board then named Willie Walsh, a former chief of British Airways and of the airline association IATA. He took charge in August 2026.

## [22:05] What the test taught

Here is what I take from it.
The same discipline that made IndiGo punctual also made it fragile. A design tuned for maximum use has no slack. In a normal week, slack looks like waste: a spare pilot at home, an aircraft not flying. In a bad week, slack is the only thing that lets the system bend.
The engine crisis was a shock the airline could plan around, and it bent. The new rest rules were a change it had been warned about, and it had not built the room to absorb them.
This is not a story about heroes or villains. It is a story about design. A good design bends rather than breaks. And bending needs room.
I should add one fact, so the picture is complete. By April 2026, IndiGo's share of domestic passengers was back at about sixty-five per cent. Customers came back. The promise still meant something. But the airline paid for the lesson in money, in reputation and in leadership.

## [23:10] What this means for a firm of 15 to 100 people

You do not run an airline. Your firm may have forty people, one factory or one office, and a customer list you know by name. So let me translate what we have seen into four lessons. Each one comes from a moment in the story you have just watched.

## [23:30] Lesson one: one promise your customer can check

First, pick one promise your customer can check, and design the work backwards from it.
IndiGo's promise could be checked with a wristwatch. Yours might be: every enquiry gets a quotation within one working day. Or: every order leaves the factory on the date we confirmed. Or: every client file is ready for review a week before the deadline.
Now work backwards. If the quotation must go in one day, who receives the enquiry? Where is it written down? Who prices it, and by what time? Who checks it before it goes? The promise tells you what the steps must be, the way the departure time tells the ground crew when the doors must close.
Most firms do the opposite. They describe the steps they already have, and hope the promise comes out of them.
Remember the order of IndiGo's decisions. The promise came first. The aircraft type, the turn and the number all followed from it. In your firm, write the promise down before you write a single step. Then test every step against it.

## [24:40] Lesson two: standardise what repeats, and say no to the rest

Second, standardise what repeats, so that anyone can run it. And treat complexity as a cost you pay every day.
IndiGo's single aircraft type meant any pilot could fly any plane. In your firm, the equivalent is one way to do each repeating job. One format for a quotation. One dispatch checklist. One place where every task sits, with a name, a date and a next step. When the way of working lives on a sheet that anyone can open, a new person can run it in their second week. When it lives in your head, it leaves the building with you every evening.
And say no. Every special case you accept is a second aircraft type. Before you agree to one, ask a single question. Will this make the promise easier to keep, or harder? If it makes it harder, the answer is no, or not yet.
And if you must say yes, do what IndiGo did with its turboprops. Put a fence around it. Give the special case its own owner and its own checklist, so that it does not leak into the main work and slow everything else down.

## [26:00] Lesson three: the number every day, the reasons every week

Third, watch the one number every day, and the reasons every week.
The regulator publishes IndiGo's on-time share every month, and nobody can argue with it. Your firm needs the same. One number for your promise. How many quotations went out on time this week. How many orders left on the date. You should be able to see it without asking anyone.
Then, once a week, look at the misses and their reasons. Was it material? An approval? A change from the customer? Someone on leave? The number tells you how you did. The reasons tell you what to fix. This is what I call the Friday score. Its partner is the Monday hand-out, where every person starts the week knowing what is theirs.
Notice one more thing about the regulator's number. It did not wait to be asked for. It arrived every month, whether the news was good or bad. Your score should work the same way. It should come to you. You should not have to go looking for it.
Without this, you find out last. A customer tells you before your own team does.

## [27:15] Lesson four: a bad year tests the design

Fourth, a bad year tests the design, and a good design bends rather than breaks.
When engine problems grounded IndiGo's aircraft, it bent. When its rosters had no slack, it broke. In your firm, slack is a second person who knows how to raise the invoice. It is two days of buffer on the dispatch date you promise. It is spare capacity in the busy month before Diwali. It looks like waste in a quiet week. It is what carries you through a hard one.
And when something does break, do what IndiGo was made to do. Write down what failed. Change the design, not just the people. Then check the change at a fixed interval until it holds. After December, the regulator required a review of IndiGo's crew use every fifteen days while the relief lasted.
[your own line]

## [28:05] Close

Think back to the apron at the start of this episode. Nobody shouting. Nobody calling the owner. Each person knowing their part, and the order in which it happens. That is not a picture of a big company. It is a picture of a design. A firm of forty people can have one too, at its own scale.
Let me end with my own work.
In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, I started with one process. Today every piece of work there has a home: a name, a date and a next step, on our own sheet. The work is handed out on Monday. The score comes back on Friday. I no longer find out last.

script:
## [00:00] The month-end rush

It is the last week of the month, in a car factory in Japan, in the early 1950s.
The conveyor is running faster than usual. The same workers are on the line. The plan says a certain number of vehicles must be built this month, and the month is nearly over.
Two weeks ago, this same line stood half idle. The parts it needed were missing. Meanwhile the machine shop next door kept making parts and sending them forward, whether anyone needed them or not. Crates piled up beside the line. The assembly area began to look like a parts warehouse.
So the first half of the month is waiting. The second half is rushing. And at the end of it, the plan is still missed.

## [00:50] The question

If you run a factory, a trading firm or a dispatch business, you may know this month. The godown is full, and still the one item the customer wants is missing. The last week is overtime and phone calls.
This episode is about how that company, short of money and short of time, designed its way out. Not with more supervisors. With a card, a cord, a question and a written page.
The question is simple. How do you make the work call for itself, so that you do not have to?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [01:30] A family that built machines

The company is Toyota. Today it is one of the largest car makers in the world. In 1950 it was nothing of the kind.
The family did not begin with cars. It began with looms. Sakichi Toyoda was an inventor of weaving machines. His son, Kiichiro Toyoda, wanted to build cars. Toyota's car plant at Koromo began operating in November 1938.
Kiichiro had an idea for that plant. Make only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed. His reasoning was plain. A car cannot be finished if one part is missing. So every part should arrive just in time. Not weeks early, sitting on the floor. Not a day late, holding up the line. Toyota still credits him with that idea.
Then came the war, and the years after it. The idea stayed mostly on paper.

## [02:30] 1950: no money for stock

By 1950, Toyota was in serious trouble. A tight money policy in Japan had brought on a recession. Costs were rising. Prices were not. In April 1950 a labour dispute broke out over layoffs. In June, Kiichiro resigned, to take responsibility for it. All of this is in Toyota's own history.
Think about what that means for a factory floor. A company that is short of cash cannot afford to make parts early and stack them. Every crate of parts sitting beside the line is money. It is money that cannot pay a wage, or a supplier, or a bank.
And yet that is exactly what the factory was doing. Each part travelled with a single slip of paper. The machine shop made what its plan said, and pushed it forward. Whether assembly needed it or not. Early in the month, assembly ran at about half its plan, because the right parts were missing. Late in the month, the line was sped up to catch up. The plan was still missed.

## [03:40] Your desk in it

Let me bring this closer to home.
In many firms, the work moves in the same way. Production makes what was planned last week. Purchase buys what it bought last month. Sales promises a date without seeing what is on the floor. Each department pushes its work to the next one, and hopes.
And who holds it together? The owner. The owner knows which customer is waiting. The owner knows which material is short. The owner remembers which cartons belong to which order. The owner is the memory, the follow-up department and the feedback loop.
So every morning starts with the owner on the phone, asking the same thing: "Ho gaya?" Is it done? Is it packed? Has it left?
[your own line]
This is not a character problem. Your people are not lazy, and they are not careless. The work has no home. Nobody can see its state without asking. And the only feedback loop in the building is you.

## [04:50] The design problem

Toyota in 1950 had the same problem, at a larger scale, with less money. It could not hire its way out. It could not afford a warehouse full of safety stock. And it could not put a manager over every machine.
So it had to design something. It needed a way for each step to know what to do next, without being told by a person. A way for a problem to show itself, without waiting to be found. A way to fix the cause, so that the problem does not come back. And a way to write the job down, so that it does not live in one head.
That is the choice every owner faces when the business outgrows one person's memory. Hire more people to chase, or change the design so that less chasing is needed.
In the next twelve minutes, I will show you each of those four pieces. Then the numbers, measured by outside researchers. And then the three times the whole system was tested hard.

## [06:00] Piece one: the shop that refills itself

The first piece came from a shop.
Taiichi Ohno ran a machine shop at Toyota. He later became the main architect of what is now called the Toyota Production System. In his own book, Toyota Production System, he says the idea came from the American supermarket.
Think about how a supermarket works. A customer takes what she needs from the shelf. The shelf is then refilled with exactly what was taken. Nobody stocks the shelf on a guess. The empty space is the order.
Ohno turned this around inside a factory. The later process is the customer. The earlier process is the shop. Assembly takes the parts it needs, when it needs them. The machine shop makes only enough to replace what was taken. Nothing more.
There is an honest wrinkle in this story. By his own account, his shop began trying the idea in 1953, and he first stood inside an American supermarket on a visit in 1956. And Toyota's official history tells it differently. It says the trigger was a 1954 trade report about a Lockheed aircraft plant in America. The two accounts do not agree, and I will not pretend they do. What matters for us is that both describe the same design.

## [07:40] The card

To make the design work, Toyota added a card. In Japanese, it is called kanban. From here on, I will just call it the card.
What is written on the card? Toyota's own history lists three things: the product name, the product number and the quantity. Standard references add three more. Where the part comes from. Where it is stored. And which process uses it.
Now watch how it moves. A container of parts sits beside the assembly line, with a card on it. When a worker opens that container, the card comes off. It goes into a small box. Someone carries it back to the shop that makes the part.
That card is now an order. Make one more container. Exactly this part. Exactly this many. When the new container is ready, the card goes back on it, and it travels forward to the line. Then the loop begins again.
Nothing is made without a card. Nothing is moved without a card. That is the whole rule.

## [09:00] What the card does

Now look at what that small card has done.
First, the work has a home. What to make next is not in the supervisor's head. It is written on a card, in a known place, and anyone can read it.
Second, the state of the work is visible. Full containers and an empty card box mean the shop is ahead. A pile of cards waiting in the box means the shop is behind. Nobody has to walk across the floor and ask.
Third, and this is the clever part, the number of cards sets the stock. If ten cards exist for a part, there can never be more than ten containers of it in the building. You do not control stock by shouting at the storekeeper. You control it by deciding how many cards exist.
Practitioners describe one more habit. Take a card out on purpose, and see what goes wrong. When stock is high, problems hide behind it. When stock is lower, the next problem shows itself, and it can be fixed.
One caution. This does not mean Toyota holds no stock. After the 2011 earthquake in Japan, it asked suppliers to hold months of certain electronic chips, because those chips take so long to arrive. The card controls stock. It does not abolish it.
For a company with no money to spare, none of this was theory. It was how it stayed alive.

## [10:40] Piece two: the loom that stopped itself

The second piece is older than the car company. It goes back to the looms.
In 1896, Sakichi Toyoda built a loom with a device that stopped the machine when a thread broke. In 1924, his Type G automatic loom carried the idea further. Toyota keeps both in its own history.
Why does a stopping loom matter? A loom that keeps running with a broken thread makes cloth that has to be thrown away. A loom that stops itself makes no bad cloth. And nobody has to stand over it, watching, because the machine tells you when it is in trouble.
Toyota calls this principle jidoka. It translates it as automation with a human touch. In plain words, the judgement is built into the work. A problem stops the work before it can spread.

## [11:40] The cord

On an assembly line, the same idea becomes a cord. Toyota calls the signal andon. From here, I will just say the cord.
The cord runs along the line, within reach of every worker. If a worker sees something wrong, she pulls it. A bolt that will not seat. A part that does not fit. A job that is running behind. She does not need permission.
Here is the part most people get wrong. Pulling the cord does not stop the factory. An alarm sounds and a light comes on above her station. That calls the team leader. The team leader has the rest of that work cycle to help fix it. Seconds, not minutes.
If the problem is fixed in time, the line never stops. If it is not, that section of the line stops at the next fixed point. And then people come, and they stay until it is solved.
So the rule is not "stop everything". The rule is: raise it now, get help now, and do not pass the problem on.

## [12:50] Two thousand pulls a week

How often is the cord pulled? In 2007, the BBC visited Toyota's plant in Georgetown, Kentucky. It reported that workers there pulled the cord about two thousand times a week. At a new Ford truck plant in Michigan, the same report said, workers pulled it about twice a week.
Please do not read that as Toyota having a thousand times more problems. Every factory has problems. The difference is how many of them are seen while they are still small. Two pulls a week does not mean two problems. It means the rest are being hidden, or carried forward, or found by the customer.
This is the feedback loop. The person who finds the problem raises it at once. The person who can fix it hears within seconds. Nobody has to wait for the plant manager to walk past.
And this is how errors are caught. The bad part does not travel down the line to the next worker, and the next, and finally to a customer's driveway. It stops where it started.

## [14:00] Piece three: ask why five times

When a problem is serious, Toyota does not stop at the first answer. Ohno's habit was to ask why, five times. He gives his own example in his book.
A machine stops. Why? A fuse blew, because of an overload.
Why was there an overload? The bearing was not lubricated enough.
Why? The lubrication pump was not pumping enough.
Why? The shaft of the pump was worn.
Why? There was no strainer on the pump, so metal scrap got in.
Now look at the choices. Stop at the first answer, and you replace the fuse. The machine runs, and stops again next month. Stop at the fourth, and you replace the pump. It wears out again. Only at the fifth do you reach the cause. Fit a strainer, and the problem does not come back.
Notice one more thing. Not one of the five answers is a person. Nobody asks who forgot to oil the machine. The questions go past the person, to the design. That is not softness. It is accuracy. If you blame the worker, you fix nothing. The next worker meets the same missing strainer.

## [15:20] Piece four: the written page

The fourth piece is the least exciting, and perhaps the most important. It is a written page at each workstation. Toyota calls it standard work.
It has three parts. The pace the customer needs. The steps of the job, in order. And the small amount of work in progress that keeps the job flowing.
Here is what surprises most owners. At Toyota, the standard is not a rule sent down from an office and framed on a wall. It is the current best way, written down so that it can be improved. The improvement has a name, kaizen. In plain words, small improvements, made every day, by the people who do the work. When an improvement works, it is written back into the standard. The page changes.
Without a written standard, there is nothing to improve. There is only each person's own way of doing it, and the owner's memory of how it ought to be done.

## [16:20] The team leader

One more role holds all of this together.
In 1988, a researcher named John Krafcik studied a plant in California that Toyota ran. He described the team leader there. A union member. Responsible for five to seven people. With no fixed job on the line. The team leader's time goes to organising the work, checking quality, maintenance and training.
That is the person who answers the cord. That is the person who knows the standard and teaches it. And that is why the work does not wait for the plant manager.
So what happens when the boss is away? The cards keep moving. The cord still calls the team leader. The standard is still at the workstation. The work goes on, because none of it lives in one person's head.

## [17:05] Did it work?

Did it work? Researchers at MIT spent five years measuring car plants around the world. Their book, The Machine That Changed the World, by James Womack, Daniel Jones and Daniel Roos, came out in 1990.
Their figures for 1989. Japanese plants in Japan built a car in 16.8 hours of assembly work, on average. Japanese-owned plants in North America took about 21 hours. American-owned plants took about 25. And for every hundred cars, the Japanese plants in Japan had fifty to sixty assembly defects. The American-owned plants had roughly eighty.
Their best-known comparison was between two plants in the mid-1980s. General Motors at Framingham, in Massachusetts, and Toyota at Takaoka, in Japan. Framingham needed nearly twice the assembly hours per car. Framingham kept about two weeks of parts on hand. Takaoka kept about two hours.
Half the hours. Fewer defects. A fraction of the stock. That is what a card, a cord, a question and a page did, over thirty years of patient work.

## [18:00] Three tests

Every system looks good in a chart. The question in this series is always the same. What happened when it broke?
Toyota's system was tested in three different ways. Could it move to another country, with other people? Could it survive a fire at the one supplier it depended on? And could it survive Toyota's own growth?

## [18:25] Test one: the worst plant

In 1982, General Motors closed its car plant in Fremont, California. The people who worked there describe it as one of the worst in the company. On a normal day, about one worker in five did not turn up. Grievances ran into the thousands. Workers were disciplined for stopping the line. These accounts come from the radio programme This American Life, which interviewed the workers and managers themselves.
In 1984, General Motors and Toyota reopened the plant together, as a joint company called NUMMI. Toyota ran the production. More than eighty-five percent of the workers had worked at the old plant. Groups of them were flown to Japan, to work on Toyota's line at Takaoka for about two weeks.
The first car came off the line in December 1984. Krafcik measured NUMMI at about forty percent more productive than a traditional General Motors plant, on a par with Toyota in Japan. The MIT book put NUMMI close to Toyota's Takaoka plant on both hours and defects, and far below Framingham.
Same country. Largely the same workers. A different design.
There is a harder lesson too. General Motors found it very slow to carry NUMMI's lessons into its other plants. A plant at Van Nuys tried the approach without Toyota's people, and closed in 1992. The tools could be copied quickly. The habits took years.

## [20:15] Test two: the fire

The second test came in 1997.
Before dawn on Saturday, the first of February, a fire broke out at a factory of Aisin Seiki, in Kariya, near Toyota's home base. That one factory made about ninety-nine percent of a small brake part called a P-valve. Every Toyota vehicle needed one.
Toyota held very little stock of it. The Wall Street Journal reported about four hours at the car plants. The researchers who later studied the fire gave figures between one and three days. Either way, the lines stopped. Observers expected weeks.
What happened next was not ordered from the top. Aisin and Toyota set up a crisis room. Firms across the supplier network, several of which had never made this part, took on pieces of the work. Denso, Taiho Kogyo, Koritsu Sangyo and Kayaba were at the centre of it. Hundreds of Denso staff worked double shifts and weekends for two weeks. The first usable valves arrived on Wednesday, the fifth of February. Production was set back by days, not weeks.

## [21:20] Why the network could move

Why could they move so fast? The researchers point to the relationships. Years of shared work, shared know-how and trust between the firms.
I would add a designer's reading. Small stocks had trained everyone to watch the flow, every day. When the flow broke, they saw it at once. Written ways of working meant that one firm could take on a step from another and begin. And trust meant they started first and talked about payment later. Reports say the suppliers were paid back afterwards.
A system with small stocks is fragile against a fire. A network with these habits recovered in days.

## [21:55] Test three: growth

The third test was the hardest, because it came from inside the company.
By 2008, Toyota had passed General Motors as the world's largest car maker. Then, in late 2009 and early 2010, it recalled about nine million vehicles worldwide. Floor mats that could trap the accelerator. Pedals that could stick. There had been fatal crashes, and the questions were serious.
On the 24th of February 2010, Akio Toyoda, the company's president, gave evidence to a committee of the United States Congress. He said Toyota's order had always been safety first, quality second and volume third, and that those priorities had become confused. He said the company had pursued "growth over the speed at which we were able to develop our people".
A ten-month study by NASA and the American road-safety regulator later found no electronic fault that could explain sudden acceleration. In 2014, Toyota agreed to pay 1.2 billion dollars to resolve a US criminal investigation into how it had disclosed the problems. I am stating only what is on the public record.
The lesson for us is in his own words. The cards and the cords did not stop working. Growth outran the people trained to run them. A system is only as strong as the people who know how to use it, and that takes time to build.

## [23:00] The honest limit

Now let me be plain about what this means for you, and what it does not.
A forty-person firm in Indore is not a car plant. You do not have a moving line. You do not have a team leader for every six people. You do not have engineers to write standards. Toyota took decades to build this, and even Toyota found that it could break.
So please do not copy the tools. Do not print cards because Toyota prints cards. The lesson is the shape of the system, not the scale.
Here are four lessons. Each one comes from a moment in this story.

## [23:40] Lesson one: let the work call for itself

Remember the card. Assembly did not phone the machine shop to ask what it was making today. The empty container asked for itself.
So ask one question in your own firm. What tells my team what to do next? If the honest answer is "I do", the work has no home.
Take dispatch. An order is confirmed. Today, someone tells someone, who tells the packing team, and you check at six in the evening. Instead, every confirmed order becomes one row. It has a name, a date and a next step. When packing is done, the row moves on to dispatch. The row is the card. It travels with the work and says what happens next.
Or take stock. Set a level for each packing material. When the count falls below it, the row turns amber. The purchase person orders without being told. The empty shelf asks for itself, just as it did in Ohno's supermarket.
The same works for a quote. A quote that has gone three days without a reply turns amber on its own, and the salesperson follows up before you have to notice.
A visible signal replaces a phone call. A card, a colour, a row turning amber. Each one does the work of the call you would otherwise make.

## [25:10] Lesson two: give everyone the right to stop and flag

Remember the cord. Two thousand pulls a week, and nobody was punished for pulling it.
In most firms, a junior person who sees a problem has two choices. Stay quiet, or call the owner. Both are bad. Staying quiet sends the mistake to the customer. Calling the owner keeps the owner as the only feedback loop.
Give everyone a third choice. A flag. In a sheet, it can be one column: blocked, and the reason. The accounts clerk who sees that an invoice does not match the order can hold the dispatch, and say why. The store person who sees a wrong grade of material can stop it at the gate.
But the cord only works because the team leader comes. So someone named must answer every flag, the same day. A flag that nobody answers teaches people to stop flagging.
Stop and fix beats chase and hope.

## [26:10] Lesson three: ask why until you reach the design

Remember the fuse and the strainer.
Take a late dispatch. Why was it late? The invoice was not ready. Why? Accounts was waiting for the rate. Why? The rate was not on the order. Why? Sales agreed it on the phone and did not write it down. Why? Because the order has no place to write the agreed rate.
Five whys, and the answer is not "Sales is careless". The answer is that the order form has no box for the rate. That is a design fix. It takes ten minutes. And it does not depend on anyone being better tomorrow than they were today.
When you stop at a person, the problem comes back with the next person. When you reach the design, it stays fixed.

## [27:05] Lesson four: write the standard so the person can improve it

Remember the page at the workstation. Written down, and improved by the people who do the work.
Most owners write nothing down. The process lives in their head, and it feels quicker to do it themselves. Some owners go the other way and write a thick manual that nobody opens. Toyota's way sits between the two. One page per job. The steps, in order. What done looks like. And room for the person who does the job to write a better way.
Take a professional firm, and a client's monthly filing. One page. Which documents come in, by which date. Who prepares, who checks. What done looks like. The junior who does it every month will see the wasted step long before you do. Let her change the page.
[your own line]
When the person who does the work can improve the standard, the standard stays alive. When the standard is alive, you can be away for a week. The Monday hand-out still goes out. The Friday score still comes back.

## [28:10] What I do now

So, four lessons. Let the work call for itself. Give everyone the right to stop and flag. Ask why until you reach the design, not the person. And write the standard so the person can improve it.
In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, we did not begin with a system for everything. We began with one process. The work got a home: a name, a date and a next step. When something is late, a row turns amber, so nobody has to ask.
This is the work I do now, with owners of businesses of fifteen to a hundred people. We set up the system on your own sheet, train your team on it, and keep it running with you.
I will not tell you that a sheet fixes a business. It does not. What it does is give the work a home, so that you can see it, and your team can see it, without a phone call. The rest is habit, built one week at a time.
Toyota's card began in one machine shop. Yours can begin with one process.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.

Thank you for watching Built to Run. I will see you next week, with another story.

script:
## [00:00] The tennis court at night

It is late at night in San Bernardino, California. The year is 1952, or early 1953. Behind a family house there is a tennis court. On it, two brothers are drawing a kitchen in chalk.
There is no kitchen. There is no food. Their crew has come over after closing time. One man stands where a grill will be and turns patties that are not there. Another walks to a fry station and back. A third reaches for buns from a rack that exists only as a line on the ground.
Each time someone takes a step too many, the brothers rub out a line and draw it again. They are designing the work before anyone designs the building.
This is how the best-known history of the company tells it. By three in the morning the layout is right. The draftsman will copy it tomorrow. That night, it rains. The red chalk runs off the court in streaks.
The drawing is gone. What the brothers learned by walking it is not. That kitchen will be copied in towns they will never visit, by people they will never meet.
So here is the question for today. What does it take for a business to work the same way when the owner is not in the room?
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [01:35] A drive-in that worked

Let me go back twelve years before that night.
In 1940, Richard and Maurice McDonald open a drive-in in San Bernardino. People call them Dick and Mac. The building is small and eight-sided. There are no seats inside. Cars pull into the lot, and carhops take the order at the car window and bring the food out on a tray.
On a weekend evening there can be 125 cars in that lot. About twenty carhops run between them. The menu has about twenty-five items, most of them barbecue.
And it works. By the middle of the 1940s the drive-in sells more than 200,000 dollars a year. The two brothers share about 50,000 dollars of profit.
Those figures come from John Love's history of the company, written with McDonald's cooperation. I rely on it for most of the early story, and I will tell you where it disagrees with the version you may have seen in a film.
So this is not a story about a business in trouble. It is a story about a business that was doing well, run by two owners who could see what it cost them to keep it that way.

## [02:55] What the brothers could see

Here is what they could see.
The carhops did not stay. They left for better pay, and every new one had to be taught again. Plates and glasses broke, or went home with customers. The crowd in the lot was mostly teenagers, and families stayed away.
None of these problems was dramatic. Each one was small. And each one landed on the brothers.
I think every owner watching knows this feeling. The business is good. The customers are happy. And yet you are the one who trains the new person. You are the one who notices the missing stock. You are the one who walks over at seven in the evening and asks the question owners across India ask every day: "ho gaya?"
Then the brothers did something useful. They sat down with three years of their own receipts. And they found that about eighty percent of their sales were hamburgers.
They were running a barbecue drive-in with twenty-five items. Their customers were buying a hamburger.
That gap, between the business you run and the business your customers buy, is where most of an owner's tiredness comes from. Every extra item is something to train, stock, check and chase.

## [04:15] Closing a business that works

In the autumn of 1948, the brothers close the drive-in. Not for a week. For three months.
They let the carhops go. They decide to rebuild the whole operation around the one thing customers actually come for.
I want to stay on this for a moment, because it is the hardest part of the story for an owner to copy. Most of us redesign while we run. We add a new form on top of the old habit. We hire one more person to follow up. We buy software and keep the old register, just in case.
The brothers stopped. They gave themselves room to design the work before they did it again.
Think about what that meant in 1948. They had a business that paid them well. Their staff depended on it. Their customers came every weekend. There was no certainty it would come back. They did it because their own receipts had shown them something. The old design would always need them standing in the middle of it. They wanted a design that needed them less.
You do not have to close your firm for three months. But you do need a few protected hours where you are not running the work, only looking at it.
And the first thing the brothers designed was not a building, or a sign, or an advertisement. It was the menu.

## [05:50] Mechanism one: the short menu

The menu goes from about twenty-five items to nine. Hamburgers. Cheeseburgers. Drinks. A few things more.
The hamburger goes from thirty cents to fifteen. And every hamburger comes with the same condiments. No choices.
The plates and glasses go. Food comes in paper bags, paper wrappers and paper cups. The customer walks up to a window and collects the order.
Now look at what each choice removes.
The short menu removes decisions at the grill. A cook who makes nine things makes them the same way every time.
The fixed condiments remove the special order. No one has to remember that the third car wanted no onion.
The paper removes the dishwasher. A whole job, gone. And with it, the cost of every broken plate.
Self-service removes the carhop, the one role the brothers could never keep filled.
A note on the price, too. Halving the price only works if the cost of making each burger falls with it. Fewer items. Less waste. No dishwasher. No carhops. The low price was a result of the design, not a bet on crowds alone.
None of this is about speed for its own sake. Each choice takes away a place where the work could vary. When the work cannot vary much, a new person can do it well. That is the quiet idea under everything that follows.

## [07:25] Mechanism two: the kitchen drawn around the steps

Then they rebuild the kitchen around the work.
Two grills, each six feet long, replace a standard three-foot grill. Dick McDonald designs a steel turntable that holds twenty-four buns, so one person can dress them in a row. A local machinist builds a hand pump that puts the same measure of ketchup and mustard on every bun.
The crew is split into stations. Three on the grill. Two on shakes. Two on fries. Two dressing buns. Three at the counter. Each person has one job, and a fixed place to do it.
They call it the Speedee Service System. The target is to hand over an order in thirty seconds or less.
And here is the part people leave out. When they reopen, business falls to about a fifth of what it was. It takes about six months to come back. By 1951 the restaurant takes 277,000 dollars, nearly forty percent more than the old drive-in.
Six months of worse numbers. Every owner who has changed a working process knows those months. The brothers held their nerve.
Now, the tennis court. You will often hear that the chalk drawing happened in 1948. The film The Founder shows it that way. Love's history, and the architectural historian Alan Hess, place it a few years later, in 1952 and 1953. By then the brothers wanted a new building that other people could copy. So before the architect drew a single wall, they drew the kitchen on the court and walked the crew through it. The building, with its golden arches, was designed around that kitchen.
That is the order. The work first. The building second.

## [09:15] The gap the brothers left

The brothers did sell franchises themselves, before anyone else came along.
Each buyer received a manual of fifteen pages, a set of building plans, the right to the name, and one week of training in San Bernardino.
After that, as Love puts it, they could run their stores as they chose. And most did.
Prices differed from town to town. Some added items to the menu. One owner reshaped the arches into a point and gave the place a different name. Few of them were as clean as the original. Few sold as much.
This is worth noticing. The brothers had designed the work beautifully. In their own restaurant, under their own eyes, it ran to the second. But the design lived where they lived. Nobody was checking the other kitchens. Nobody found out when something slipped, until it showed in the sales.
That is the owner's problem in one sentence. The system worked where the owner could see it. Away from the owner, it drifted.
In the words I use with owners, the brothers were still the feedback loop. And a feedback loop that is one person's eyes cannot travel.

## [10:35] Mechanism three: one store at a time

In 1954 a salesman named Ray Kroc notices something odd. He sells a milkshake machine called the Multimixer. One small restaurant in California keeps ordering more of them. In Love's account, the order is for their ninth and tenth.
He flies out to see why. At lunch he finds queues at the windows, and orders handed over in about fifteen seconds.
He asks the brothers for the right to sell franchises across the country, and they agree. The terms are modest. A franchise costs 950 dollars. The franchisee pays 1.9 percent of sales as a service fee, and half a percent of that goes to the brothers.
On 15 April 1955, Kroc opens his own restaurant in Des Plaines, Illinois, as a model for buyers to visit. McDonald's still dates its founding to that day.
Then he makes a decision that matters more than any fee. Other chains at the time sell whole territories. One buyer pays a large sum and gets a city, or a state. Kroc refuses. He sells one store at a time.
His reason, as Love records it, is control. If a man owns the territory, he owns the business in that area, and he can ignore the standard. If a man owns one store and wants a second, he has to earn it.
The unit of the franchise is the unit of the standard. Keep that idea. It comes back.

## [12:15] Mechanism four: the manual

The person who writes the standard down is Fred Turner. He starts as one of the first grill men at Des Plaines. Within months he is writing manuals for franchisees.
His first is fifteen pages, typed and copied. The next is thirty-eight. In 1958 he produces a printed, bound manual of seventy-five pages.
Listen to the level of detail.
A quarter of an ounce of onion on each patty. French fries cut nine thirty-seconds of an inch thick. Cooking times. Temperature settings. Any meat or potatoes held more than ten minutes in the serving bin are thrown away. The grill man lays the patties from left to right, six rows of six, and turns the third row first.
About ten pages are forms. Inventory. Cash. Staff schedules.
And the opening line, as Love quotes it: "Herein outlined is the successful method."
Notice what kind of document this is. It is not a policy. It does not say "maintain high standards". It says nine thirty-seconds of an inch. A young man on his first day can read it and do the step. So can a manager in another state who has never met Kroc.
That is where the work lives at McDonald's. Not in the best cook's memory. On the page, and in the layout of the kitchen.
And look at the ten-minute rule again. It does two jobs. It catches an error before it reaches the customer. And it makes the state of the work visible. Anyone can look at the bin and the clock and see whether the rule is being kept.

## [14:00] Mechanism five: the grade in the corner

A manual is only half of it. Someone has to check.
Turner builds an inspection report. The first version is seven pages, single-spaced. Cleanliness. Food quality. Cooking times and temperatures. How long service takes.
Kroc will not read seven pages. So Turner puts a letter grade, A to F, in the top right corner.
This is how QSC begins. Quality, service, cleanliness. In the middle of the 1960s Kroc adds a V, for value.
One detail I like. Operators were never formally graded on value, because franchisees set their own prices. You grade what the operator controls.
And the grade has a consequence. By the middle of the 1960s it decides whether an operator may open another store. By the 1990s, Love writes, more than 330 field consultants each look after about twenty-one restaurants, and visit several times a year. A B is the minimum to grow.
So here is the feedback loop. The owner does not have to ask. A person who is not the owner walks into the kitchen, times the service, looks at the bin, checks the floor, and writes a grade anyone can read.
Think about what the grade does for Kroc. He cannot stand in hundreds of kitchens. He can read hundreds of letters. The grade turns a seven-page visit into one mark a busy owner can act on. That is the whole job of a report.
That is a standard a stranger can check.

## [15:40] Hamburger University, and the system underneath

In February 1961 the company opens a school in the basement of a new restaurant in Elk Grove Village, near Chicago. Fifteen people in the first class. They call it Hamburger University.
The first course runs two weeks. Potato varieties. The meat formula. How each machine works, taught on cut-away models. By 2011 the company says more than 275,000 people have graduated, taught in twenty-eight languages.
Notice why the school matters. A manual tells you what to do. Training makes sure the person at the grill has seen it done, and has done it, before a customer is waiting. The manual and the school are one design. The step, written down. And the step, practised.
In the same year, 1961, Kroc buys out the brothers for 2.7 million dollars. How that sale was handled, and how the brothers felt about it, is still argued over. I am not going to take a side.
One more layer, briefly. From 1956, Kroc's finance man, Harry Sonneborn, leased the land under each restaurant and rented it on to the franchisee at a markup. It gave McDonald's an income that did not depend on fees. It is the financial system under the operating system. It matters to McDonald's. It does not matter to your firm.

## [17:10] Five answers so far

So before we go to India, the five questions.
Where does the work live? On the page, and in the layout. How can anyone see its state? The thirty-second target, the ten-minute bin, the grade in the corner. What is the feedback loop? The consultant's visit, and a grade that decides the next store. How are errors caught? Fixed portions, discard times, inspections.
And what happens when the owner is away? At McDonald's the owner is always away. Kroc never met most of the people running his kitchens.
Notice what is missing from that list. Kroc standing at the counter. The brothers watching the grill. The design does not need the owner in the kitchen. It needs the owner at the design, and at the review.

## [18:00] Six years before the first burger

Now the test. And I want to take it somewhere close to home.
McDonald's opens in India in October 1996, at Basant Lok in Vasant Vihar, New Delhi. A restaurant at Bandra in Mumbai follows the same month.
Two Indian partners run it. In the north and east, Connaught Plaza Restaurants, a joint venture led by Vikram Bakshi. In the west and south, Hardcastle Restaurants, led by Amit Jatia. Jatia, by his own account, is a vegetarian running a family industrial business when a friend suggests the partnership. He goes on to train at Hamburger University.
The menu is redesigned for India. No beef. No pork. It is the first McDonald's to serve neither. There is a wide vegetarian range.
And the kitchen is redesigned too. Vegetarian and non-vegetarian food are kept apart all the way from the processing plant to the restaurant kitchen. That is not a line on a poster. It is a line on the floor, the way the brothers drew theirs.
But the part that interests me most is the timing. The company says it spent six years building the supply chain before the first restaurant opened. Six years of work before one rupee of sales.

## [19:25] Lettuce, potatoes and a truck with three temperatures

Take lettuce. When McDonald's arrives, iceberg lettuce is imported. In India it grows in a window of about sixty days a year.
By its own account, the company spends three years finding the right places to grow it. It trains five to six hundred farmers. It writes farming process manuals in several languages. And it audits the farms against the standard.
Listen to that again. Process manuals, and audits. It is Fred Turner's 1958 manual, taken to a farm.
Potatoes take longer. Until 2007, the fries are imported. Work on a suitable potato in Gujarat begins in 2004. The first Indian-grown fry potato arrives in 2007. It takes about six more years before every order of fries uses Indian potatoes.
And none of it works without cold. In 1997 the company brings in trucks with three zones. Frozen, at minus eighteen. Chilled, at one to four degrees. And dry. Where a restaurant has no proper loading dock, the cases are covered with thermal blankets to hold their temperature for the fifteen or twenty minutes from truck to kitchen.
The early suppliers are Indian companies, several in partnership with McDonald's global vendors. Patties from Taloja. Cheese from Baramati. Lettuce from Talegaon. A cold-chain distributor serving the restaurants.
This is the India version of the chalk drawing. Before they served a single customer, they designed the work all the way back to the farm.

## [21:00] The test: when the partnership broke

Every system is tested. In north and east India, the test was a dispute between partners. I will tell it only as the public record does, because the people involved are living, and the matter is settled.
In 2013 McDonald's voted against Vikram Bakshi's re-election as managing director of Connaught Plaza Restaurants, the fifty-fifty joint venture. A long legal dispute followed.
From June 2017, 43 of the joint venture's Delhi restaurants were shut after their eating-house licences expired. In July 2017 the National Company Law Tribunal reinstated Bakshi as managing director. In August 2017 McDonald's India ended the franchise agreements for all 169 restaurants, citing unpaid royalties and other obligations. The joint venture disputed that. In December 2017 the logistics partner said it would stop supplies, and about eighty restaurants faced closure.
In May 2019 the two sides settled out of court, and McDonald's bought Bakshi's stake.

## [22:00] What failed first, and what came back first

I want to draw two things from this. Neither is a judgement on any person.
First, look at what failed. The restaurants did not close because anyone forgot how to make a burger. The manual was still there. They closed when licences lapsed, and others faced closure when the cold chain stopped. The parts of the system that depend on a working relationship failed first.
Second, look at how the recovery began. With the settlement, McDonald's closed the north and east restaurants temporarily, to reopen over about two weeks. The reason it gave was a comprehensive assessment of operational protocols and employee training. It began with a review of how the work was done and how people were trained.
There is a lesson for an owner even here. Your system includes your suppliers, your licences and your partners. A manual cannot protect you from a broken relationship. What it can do is show you, quickly, where the break is.
That is question six. What happened when it broke? The first step back was a review of the standard.

## [23:05] Where the comparison stops

Now let me speak to you directly, as the owner of a business of fifteen or a hundred people.
First, the honest limit. McDonald's today has more than 45,000 restaurants, most of them run by franchisees. It owns land. It spent six years and a great deal of capital in India before it sold a burger. Your firm will do none of that, and it does not need to.
I also want to be careful. I am not saying a forty-person firm should behave like a franchise. Your clients know you. Your team knows you. That is a strength. The point is only that what you know should not live in you alone.
Michael Gerber's book The E-Myth Revisited uses McDonald's as its central example of a business designed as a prototype, built to be repeated by people who are not the founder. That is the useful idea. Not the size. The manual and the standard.
So here are four things I take from this story.

## [24:15] Lesson one: design the work, then cut the menu

One. Design the work before you buy the building.
The brothers drew the kitchen before the architect drew the walls. In your firm, the building is the software, the new hire, the bigger office. Before any of those, take one process. An enquiry becoming a quote. An order becoming a dispatch. Draw it on paper. Every step, every handover, every person. Then walk it, the way the crew walked the tennis court.
And while you draw it, cut the menu. The brothers went from twenty-five items to nine, so each one could be made the same way every time. Many firms offer every client something slightly different. Five ways to quote. Three ways to confirm an order. Each variation is a place where the work depends on one person's memory. Cut it until it can be done the same way every time.

## [25:15] Lesson two: write the step for day one

Two. Write the step so a new person can do it on day one.
Fred Turner did not write "cook the fries well". He wrote nine thirty-seconds of an inch, and ten minutes in the bin.
In your firm, that means the dispatch checklist says which documents go in the envelope, in which order, and who signs. The client file says what is due, on what date, and what the next step is. Work needs a home. A name, a date, a next step.
If your best person is the only one who knows how a quote is priced, the work lives in their memory. That is not their fault. It is a design that has not been done yet.
[your own line]

## [26:05] Lesson three: a standard a stranger can check

Three. A standard is something a stranger can check.
QSC worked because a consultant who had never met the operator could walk in and give a grade. That is the test I would put to any rule in your office.
If you wrote "follow up with clients promptly", nobody can check it. If you wrote "every enquiry gets a quote within two working days, and the sheet shows the date it went", anyone can check it. Your accountant can. Your son or daughter can. A new manager can, in the first week.
And grade what people control. McDonald's never graded value, because operators set the prices. Do not score your dispatch team on a delay the transporter caused.
Try it with one process this week. Write three rules for it. Then ask someone who does not do that work to check them on Friday. If they cannot tell whether a rule was kept, the rule needs rewriting, not the person.

## [27:10] Lesson four: the design and the Friday review

Four. The owner's job is the design and the Friday review, not the counter.
The brothers were brilliant at the counter. In their own restaurant, nothing slipped. But their licensees drifted, because the only loop was the brothers' own eyes. Kroc and Turner built something else. A manual. A visit. A grade. And a rule that the grade decides what happens next.
For a firm of forty people, that looks very ordinary. On Monday, the work is handed out, each item with a name, a date and a next step. On Friday, the score comes back. What was done. What is late. What is stuck. You read one screen. You stop being the follow-up department. You stop finding out last.
Start with one process. That is how the brothers started too. One menu. One kitchen. One tennis court.

## [28:10] What I do now

The brothers' chalk washed away in one night of rain. What lasted was what they learned by walking it. Where each step belongs. Who does it. How you know it was done.
I have spent a long time with this story, because it is so often told as a story about a salesman, or about a brand. To me it is a story about a manual and a grade. Two brothers designed the work. The people after them designed the loop.
In my family's firm, VSP Consultants, I learned this the slow way. The work lived in people's heads. The owner was the memory, the follow-up department and the feedback loop. So I designed our system on our own sheet. Where each piece of work lives, who has it, when it is due, and the score on Friday. The firm runs on it every day.
This is the work I do now, for owners of businesses with fifteen to a hundred people. We start with one process. We set it up on your own sheet, train your team on it, and keep it running. Your team still does the work. On the first call, I show you one live system, on a demo copy with invented data, so you can judge it for yourself.
If you want to see how this looks for your business, book a 30-minute call. The link is in the description.
Thank you for watching Built to Run.
