script:
## [00:00] Cold open: Wednesday, ten to three

It is Wednesday afternoon in a clothes shop in Spain. The clock on the back wall says ten to three.
The manager walks the rails. A white shirt has sold out in medium. A dress has gone in two sizes. Three customers this week asked for a jacket in a darker colour, and the shop does not have it.
She types her order into a handheld device. The deadline is three o'clock. If she misses it, she waits until Saturday.
By Friday, a truck will bring what she asked for. Not a season's worth. A few pieces of each. Enough for the next few days. Then she will order again.
This happens in every shop of the company, twice a week, every week, at fixed times. It has worked this way for more than twenty years. The company is Zara.

## [00:58] The question

Most businesses order the way they always have. Once a season, on a feeling, in a large lot.
Zara orders twice a week, on a fixed clock, in small lots, based on what sold.
That one habit helped a shop in a small Spanish city become one of the largest clothing businesses in the world. Today I want to show you how that habit works, and how a trader or distributor with forty people can run the same rhythm on a sheet.
This is Built to Run. Stories of businesses that run on systems, not on memory.

## [01:38] Act 1: The bet every trader places

Let me start with a problem you already know.
Every season, you place a bet. Before Diwali. Before the wedding season. Before summer. You commit money to stock months before a single customer walks in.
Some of that stock flies. You run out by the second week, and the customer goes next door. Some of it does not move at all. It sits in the godown. By March it is on a discount table, or it is still sitting there.
Then the season itself becomes a chase. Which branch needs what. What came in. What is stuck. Why the count in the godown does not match the book. And all of those questions come to one desk. Yours.
The bet has a price that never shows up as one line in the accounts. It is the money sitting in cartons instead of in the bank. It is the interest on the limit you drew to buy them. It is the discount you give in March to get some of that money back. And it is the sale you lost in October, when the thing the customer wanted was not on the shelf.
Most owners accept this as the nature of trade. Zara treated it as a design problem.

## [03:04] The owner's desk

Picture a distributor in Indore. Forty people. Two godowns and a counter.
The order to the company goes in when the owner remembers, or when a salesman shouts that something is finished. The quantity is what was ordered last time, plus a little extra, to be safe.
The counter staff know things the owner does not. They know that three customers asked for a pack size you do not stock. They know a new shade is moving. But that knowledge stays at the counter. It goes home with them at eight.
And when the owner walks in the next morning, he asks the same question he asked yesterday. "Order ho gaya?"
None of this is laziness. Everyone is working hard. The problem is that the order has no fixed day, no fixed rule and no home for what the counter knows. So the owner becomes the memory, the follow-up department and the feedback loop, all at once.
[your own line]

## [04:11] Where Zara began

Zara began with exactly that problem.
Amancio Ortega started making clothes in a small workshop in A Coruña, a port city in the north-west of Spain, in 1963. In 1975 he opened the first Zara shop in the same city.
The story the company's admirers tell is that a German buyer cancelled a large order of lingerie. Ortega's money was stuck in unsold goods. So he opened a shop near his factory and sold them himself. That story is repeated in Harvard Business Review. Treat it as the company's own legend, not as an audited fact.
What is on the record is the lesson he seems to have drawn. Stock nobody ordered is the most expensive thing a clothing business can own.

## [05:02] How far it went

Here is how far that shop went.
Inditex, the group that owns Zara, was formed in 1985 and listed on the Madrid stock exchange in 2001.
In 2008 it had 4,264 stores and sales of about 10.4 billion euros. By 2012, 6,009 stores and nearly 16 billion euros. In 2025, about 5,460 stores and nearly 40 billion euros of sales. These figures are from the company's own annual reports.
Notice one thing. After 2019 the number of stores went down, and sales kept going up. Fewer, larger shops. A large online business. And underneath all of it, the same rhythm of ordering, shop by shop, twice a week.
So how does that rhythm work? I am going to show it to you as five plain mechanisms.

## [05:54] Act 2, mechanism one: A fixed clock

The first mechanism is a fixed clock.
Inditex says it distributes to its stores twice a week, and that every shipment brings new models. Researchers from MIT and UCLA who worked with the company describe the same thing: two central warehouses in Spain shipping directly to every Zara store in the world, twice a week.
The ordering deadlines were fixed too. As reported in Harvard Business Review in 2004, shops in Spain and southern Europe ordered by three in the afternoon on Wednesday, and by six in the evening on Saturday. Shops in the rest of the world ordered by three on Tuesday and six on Friday.
And the deadline was real. A shop that missed Wednesday waited until Saturday.
The exact days and times may have changed since then. The company does not publish them today. But the principle has not changed.
Then the goods move on a schedule too. Inditex says stock reaches European stores about thirty-six hours after the order is received at the distribution centre. Stores in the Americas and Asia, within forty-eight hours.
Why does a fixed clock matter so much?
Because everyone downstream can plan around it. The factory knows when cutting has to finish. The warehouse knows when the trucks leave. The shop knows when new stock will come and when to clear space for it.
Nobody has to call anybody to ask. The clock answers the question.
There is a second effect, and it is easy to miss. A fixed clock makes every order small. If you know another delivery is coming on Saturday, you do not need to over-order on Wednesday. The fear that drives the extra cartons, "what if we run out", is answered by the next order day. The rhythm itself takes the panic out of the quantity.
Now think of your own order to the company, or to your supplier. When does it go? If the answer is "when it is needed", then the answer is really "when someone remembers". A fixed day is the first home you can give that work.

## [08:17] Mechanism two: The counter is the sensor

The second mechanism is the one I find most beautiful as a designer. Zara treats the shop as a sensor.
Most companies try to forecast demand from the head office. They look at last year's numbers and make a guess.
Zara listens to the counter instead. Inditex says its design teams build each season's models from market trends and from customer feedback that comes through its stores. More than seven hundred designers work on its collections.
Accounts of the company from the early 2000s describe how that worked in practice. At the head office in Arteixo, near A Coruña, designers sat with the people who handled each region's shops and with the buyers who planned production. Store managers reported what customers asked for and could not find. A colour. A length. A size. That report went to the people deciding the next order and the next design.
There is a quiet rule on the shop floor too. When a key size of an article runs out in a shop, the article comes off display. A shirt rail without medium and large does not sell, so it is better to pull it and wait for the next delivery. That rule makes the state of the stock visible on the floor itself. Anyone walking past can see which article needs sizes.
So there are two signals. What sold, which the till records. And what was asked for and was not there, which only the person at the counter knows.
In most businesses the second signal is lost every evening. At Zara it had a home and a reader.
Think about what that means in a hardware shop, or a paint dealer, or a garment wholesaler in Indore. The till, or the billing software, tells you what sold. It cannot tell you about the customer who asked for a size you did not have and walked out. That sale never enters any book. Only the person at the counter saw it happen. If nobody asks them, and nobody writes it down, the business learns nothing from it.

## [10:39] Mechanism three: Small lots, ordered to what sold

The third mechanism is small lots, ordered to what sold.
Inditex says it keeps a low stock commitment at the start of each season, so that it can respond to demand during the season. In plain words: it does not bet the whole season on day one. It makes a first, small run. It watches what sells. Then it makes more of what sold, and stops making what did not.
That habit has a cost and a reward. The cost is that some popular items run out. The reward is that articles are almost never discounted during the regular season.
Here is what the research supports. The MIT and UCLA researchers describe Zara's articles as almost never discounted during the regular selling season. They cite a Harvard Business School case from 2003 for that point. You will see sharper percentages quoted online. They cannot be traced to a primary source, so I will not repeat them.
And to be fair, Zara still has a sale. In 2008 its clearance sales brought in more than a billion euros. The system does not abolish the sale. It keeps it to the end of each season.
Now, the order itself. For years, store managers set their own quantities, size by size, and a team at the warehouse reconciled them. The researchers noticed something every owner will recognise. The managers could not see how much stock the warehouse held, and the warehouse team usually lowered what they asked for. The request was honest, but it was not a clean signal of demand.
So, working with Zara's own team, they built a model. It forecast each article's sales in each shop, by size, over the next few days, and shared the available stock across the whole network. In a controlled pilot in 2006, the new process raised sales by three to four percent and kept products on display for longer. Zara then used it for all its products worldwide.
The store manager's knowledge stayed in the loop. The guesswork in the quantity was taken out.
What is a small lot for you? It depends on your supplier and your margin. For one trader it is ten cartons instead of forty. For another it is one week of stock instead of one month. The test is simple. If the item stops selling tomorrow, how long will the last order sit on your shelf? If the answer is three months, the lot was too big.

## [13:32] Mechanism four: Fast movers close, slow movers far

The fourth mechanism is about where things are made and where they wait.
If you want to order twice a week, your supply has to be able to answer twice a week. So Zara keeps a large part of its production close to home.
In its 2021 annual report, Inditex said half of the factories making its garments were in Spain, Portugal, Morocco and Turkey. In 2022, forty-nine percent. In its 2025 results, the company describes this as sourcing close to home, within the season.
The company also says something important about which goods are made where. The most fashion-sensitive garments come from these nearby suppliers, or from its own factories in Spain. Longer-lived basics, the things that sell steadily all year, can be made further away, where it is cheaper and slower.
Fast movers close. Slow movers far. That is the whole rule.
Then all of it passes through central logistics in Spain, with the main centre at Arteixo, next to the head office. Goods arrive, are sorted by shop and leave again, to reach Europe in about a day and a half and the rest of the world in about two days.
Notice that this is a trade. Making things close to home costs more per piece. Zara accepts that cost on the goods where speed matters most, because a fast answer to demand saves more than it costs. On the goods where speed does not matter, it buys cheaper and slower.
For a distributor in Indore, the same rule reads differently but works the same way. The item that sells every day belongs at the counter and in the branch. The item that sells once a month belongs in the central godown, counted, waiting to be called.

## [15:30] Mechanism five: Count honestly, and often

The fifth mechanism is the one most owners skip. Count honestly, and count often.
An order built on what sold is only as good as your count. If the book says ten and the shelf has four, every decision after that is wrong.
In 2014, Inditex's chief executive, Pablo Isla, told shareholders that about seven hundred of its stores were already using radio tags on garments, and that around five hundred more would be added every year. The tags let staff check an incoming delivery and count a shop's stock far faster and more accurately, and they flag which garments need reordering.
By the end of 2020, Inditex said those tags, and a single stock record shared by its stores and its website, were in place across all its brands.
In 2019, Isla put the thinking in one line. "Our business model has always been based on very low inventory."
Why does a count drift in the first place? Not because people are dishonest. Because goods move in ways the book does not see. A carton is returned and put on the wrong shelf. A sample is given away. A wrong code is billed. Each small slip is harmless. Over a season they add up to a book nobody trusts, and an owner who walks into the godown to check for himself.
You do not need radio tags. You need a count you trust, done on a fixed day, by a named person, with the difference written down.

## [17:13] What happens when the owner is away

Let me put the five mechanisms through the questions this series always asks.
Where does the work live? In a fixed order cycle and a shared record of each shop's stock, not in one person's head.
How can anyone see the state of the work? The deadline is visible. The truck either came or it did not. The rail with missing sizes shows it on the floor.
What is the feedback loop? The counter reports, twice a week, to the people who decide what to make.
How are errors caught? By a model that checks the request against what actually sold, and by a count that does not depend on memory.
And what happens when the owner is away? Amancio Ortega stepped down as chairman in 2011. In 2011 the group sold about 13.8 billion euros. In 2025, nearly 40 billion. The orders went in twice a week, whoever sat in the chair.

## [18:17] Act 3: The test. A country in recession

Every system looks good in a good year. So let us look at the bad years.
The first test was Spain itself. After 2008, Spain went into a deep recession. By the start of 2013, about twenty-seven percent of Spanish workers were unemployed. That is from Spain's own statistics office.
Zara's home market was in trouble. And yet, between 2008 and 2012, Inditex grew its sales from about 10.4 billion euros to nearly 16 billion. It went from 4,264 stores to 6,009.
Spain's share of its store sales fell from twenty-five percent to twenty-one percent in a single year. So growth came from abroad, while the home market shrank as a share.
I want to be careful here. A twice-weekly order does not create growth on its own. But it meant each shop was stocked to what its own customers bought, in a year when Spanish customers were buying less. A shop that orders what sold does not drown in a recession. It simply orders less.
Every owner watching this has lived through a slow year. A market that goes quiet for six months. A big customer who stops paying. In a slow year, the business that ordered big in advance is stuck with the stock and the loan behind it. The business that orders every few days feels the slowdown in its next order, not in its godown. It loses sales, like everyone else. It does not also lose its cash.

## [19:57] The pandemic

The second test was harder. In the first three months of the 2020 financial year, up to eighty-eight percent of Inditex's stores were closed at some point.
Sales in that quarter fell forty-four percent. The group reported a loss of 409 million euros. Much of that loss came from a one-off provision for a plan to close or absorb between one thousand and twelve hundred smaller stores.
Look at the stock. At the end of April 2020, inventory was ten percent lower than a year before. That is what you would expect when shops order what sold. When selling stopped, ordering slowed with it.
And the stores became small warehouses. Staff packed online orders from their own stockrooms. That depends on knowing exactly what is in each stockroom, and that is what the tags and the single stock record across stores and website gave them.
For the full year 2020, sales fell twenty-eight percent to about 20.4 billion euros. Profit fell seventy percent. But online sales grew seventy-seven percent. The company says the single stock record alone added 1.2 billion euros of online sales, and that its supply chain kept running normally because so much of it was close to home.
Days of stock rose to about ninety-four that year. By 2025 they were back to about seventy-one.
What does this test tell us? Not that the system made Zara immune. It did not. The company lost money in a quarter for the first time as a listed business. But the system bent instead of breaking. The order cycle shrank when sales shrank. The stock was in one record, so it could be sold through a different door. And, by the company's own account, the supply close to home kept moving. A business that runs on a rhythm can slow the rhythm down. A business that runs on one big bet has already placed it.

## [22:07] The honest limits

There is a third test, and it is not about stock. It is about the people and the planet behind the model. I want to state it as plainly as the record allows.
In 2011, Brazilian labour authorities found workers in degrading conditions at workshops in São Paulo making Zara garments through an outsourced supplier. Zara said that outsourcing was unauthorised and in breach of its code of conduct.
In 2017, shoppers in Istanbul found notes in Zara garments from workers at a supplier's factory that had closed owing them wages. Inditex said it had met its contractual obligations and was working with other brands on a hardship fund for the workers.
And there is the wider argument about fast fashion. Global clothing production roughly doubled between 2000 and 2015, according to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. Critics argue that a model built on frequent new styles makes people buy more and wear each piece less.
I am not here to settle that debate. I am here to look at one narrow thing: how a business decides what to order, and when. That part is worth learning from. The rest is worth knowing, so that we learn the right thing.

## [23:25] Act 4: What this means for a business of forty people

Now let me speak to you directly, as the owner of a business with fifteen or a hundred people.
You are not Inditex. You do not have two warehouses in Spain, seven hundred designers, or researchers from MIT writing models for you. Nobody is asking you to.
But every mechanism we just saw started as a habit before it became software. A fixed day. A small order. A report from the counter. An honest count. Those are habits any shop or distributor can run on a sheet.
Here are four. Each one comes from a moment in the story you have just seen.
And one more thing before we start. Do not try all four in the same week. Start with one process. The order to your main supplier, or the stock of your twenty fastest items. Run it for a month. Then add the next.

## [24:25] Lesson one: Fix the order day and the delivery day, and keep them

Remember the Zara manager watching the clock at ten to three on Wednesday.
Choose your order days. Two a week is a good start. Tuesday and Friday, for example. Write them down. Tell your supplier, your godown and your branches.
Then agree the delivery day that follows each order. And keep both, even in a busy week. Especially in a busy week.
What changes is that nobody has to ask "has the order gone?" The day answers it. If an order is late, everyone can see it is late, because the day has passed.
For a trader, that is the order to the company. For a manufacturer, it is the raw material order. For a firm like ours, it is the day the week's work is handed out.
If your supplier cannot deliver on a fixed day today, start with your own side. Fix the day you send the order. The supplier usually follows a customer who is predictable.

## [25:31] Lesson two: Order what sold, in small lots

Remember the first small run, and the second order based on what actually sold.
On your order day, the order is simple. Look at what sold since the last order. Look at what is on the shelf. Order to refill what sold, not what you hope will sell.
Here is an example, with invented numbers. You sold twelve cartons of an item since Friday. You keep a level of fifteen on the shelf. You have three left. So you order twelve. Not twenty, because the salesman is confident. Not thirty, because a scheme is running. Twelve, because twelve sold.
That means smaller orders, more often. It feels risky at first. You worry about running out. But a business that orders twice a week can correct itself twice a week. A business that orders once a season can correct itself once a season.
And keep Zara's rule about place. Fast movers close: at the counter, in the branch, in the van. Slow movers far: in the central godown, counted, called when needed.

## [26:42] Lesson three: Make the counter the sensor, and give its report a home

Remember the store manager reporting what customers asked for and could not find.
Your counter staff hear things every day that you never hear. A pack size. A colour. A brand a customer named. Today that knowledge goes home with them.
Give it a home. One column on a sheet, or one page in a notebook at the counter. "Asked for, not in stock." Date, item, how many times. Two minutes a day.
Then read it on order day. Not once a month. On order day, next to what sold.
The counter becomes the sensor. And the person at the counter learns that what they notice changes what the business buys. That is a quiet kind of respect, and staff feel it.

## [27:33] Lesson four: Count honestly, and often

Remember the tags on every garment, and the single stock record during the pandemic.
You do not need tags. You need a count you trust. Pick your fast movers, maybe twenty items. Count them every week, on a fixed day, by a named person. Write down the difference between the book and the shelf.
The first few weeks, the differences will surprise you. That is not bad news. It is the first honest number you have had.
Do not punish the person who finds the difference. If finding a gap gets someone shouted at, gaps stop being found. Thank them, write the reason next to the number, and fix the cause.
Every order you place after that is built on something true.
